item.title: Amelia Earhart expedition heads to Pacific atoll hoping to find her plane
item.description: A US-based team of marine archaeologists has set sail for a tiny island in the far western Pacific seeking to examine the latest tantalizing clue to one of the 20th century's great unsolved mysteries: the 1937 disappearance of famed aviator Amelia Earhart.
item.dc:creator: Steve Gorman
item.content:encoded: A US-based team of marine archaeologists has set sail for a tiny island in the far western Pacific seeking to examine the latest tantalizing clue to one of the 20th century's great unsolved mysteries: the 1937 disappearance of famed aviator Amelia Earhart. Backed by Purdue University, an institution long affiliated with Earhart and her legacy, the group aims to learn whether a submerged object detected by satellite imagery in the island's lagoon six years ago is the wreckage of Earhart's twin-engine Lockheed Electra 10-E airplane. Such a finding would conclusively prove the hypothesis of some scholars that Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, crash-landed on or near the coral-ringed atoll and perished as castaways there, hundreds of miles from their intended refueling stop. After embarking from Los Angeles earlier this month, the group was expected to arrive on Tuesday, October 13, local time at Nikumaroro, an uninhabited speck of land in the remote Phoenix Islands, part of the archipelago nation of the Kiribati Republic. "Finding Amelia Earhart's Electra aircraft would be the discovery of a lifetime," Richard Pettigrew, head of the Archaeological Legacy Institute in Eugene, Oregon, who is leading the effort in conjunction with Purdue, said in press materials for the mission. Purdue general counsel and expedition member Steve Schultz, who was in Fiji conducting advance work for the expedition last week, said in an interview: "This would be solving one of the great mysteries in aviation history, certainly one of the great mysteries of the 20th century," The mission has its skeptics. Chief among them is rival Earhart explorer Ric Gillespie, co-founder of TIGHAR, short for The International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery, and author of the 2024 "One More Good Flight: The Amelia Earhart Tragedy." TREE OR PLANE? Gillespie has led a dozen expeditions of his own to the atoll over three decades and is the leading proponent of the Nikumaroro castaway theory. But he predicted the Pettigrew-Purdue team would find no airplane wreckage or anything else of consequence left on the island. The Purdue team credits Gillespie for laying the foundation of the theory they hope to prove. And they cite a compelling body of evidence that he has amassed over the years, including human artifacts recovered on the island, such as a 1930s-era glass cosmetic jar for freckle cream and remnants of a jackknife like one Earhart carried on the plane. Gillespie's investigation also encompassed modern forensic analysis from records of measurements of skeletal remains found on the island in the 1940s; logs of radio transmission bearings from distress calls picked up by wireless operators in the days immediately after Earhart vanished; and a photograph taken of the island's shoreline months later showing an object that Gillespie said appears to be the Electra's landing gear. In a Reuters interview last week, Gillespie said he believes the plane has since been lost to history, eventually swept by tides off the coral flat where it had landed largely intact and carried into the sea to sink and break apart in the surf. Two previous attempts to locate the plane's wreckage in the surrounding ocean, including a 2019 operation conducted by marine archaeologist Robert Ballard, famed for his discovery of the wreck of the Titanic, proved fruitless, Gillespie said. A plane-shaped sonar image from elsewhere on the sea floor turned out to be a pile of rocks. "I'd love to find that airplane. It ain't gonna happen," Gillespie said. Pettigrew and his team are betting otherwise. To them, the multi-branched shape first noticed in a 2020 satellite image resembles an aircraft fuselage and wings. They assert that the object, or part of it, has since been spotted in earlier aerial images of the island's lagoon dating as far back as 1938. Gillespie said he is certain that the object in question was actually a fallen pandanus tree, a palm-like evergreen native to the island region, that washed into the lagoon. "You can see the root ball. You can see the branches," Gillespie said in the interview. "It's a tree. People see what they want to see." 'GAS IS RUNNING LOW' The official US government view has long been that the Electra ran out of fuel and crashed at sea near its refueling destination of Howland Island, another dot of land about 400 miles northwest of Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner Island. Earhart was last seen taking off in her Electra on July 2, 1937, from Papua New Guinea en route to Gardner, about 2,500 miles (4,000 km) to the east, during a multi-stage attempt to become the first woman to pilot a plane around the world. Definitive radio contact with the plane was lost the next day after Earhart, 39, reported "gas is running low," followed by her final known transmission giving her geographical line of position. The disappearance spawned the largest US government search ever undertaken for a lost aircraft, including a flyover of Gardner, but no trace of the Electra or its crew was found at the time. The $900,000 Purdue mission, consisting of 17 people, plans to remain on Nikumaroro for five days before making the six-day return boat trip to the Kiribati capital, Tarawa, according to Schultz. Purdue, based in West Lafayette, Indiana, would ultimately seek to bring back any bits of the Lockheed Electra that might be recovered. Earhart was essentially a visiting faculty member at Purdue for two years as a women's career counselor and advisor to the school's aeronautics department. A Purdue research grant paid for development of the Electra, which she called her "flying laboratory." Purdue lawyer Schultz said if the plane were found, no artifacts would be removed from it on this trip. Any effort to extract the aircraft wreckage would require further permission from the Kiribati government, he said.

item.title: Mikko Rantanen, Stars ride momentum into matchup vs. Penguins
item.description: Mikko Rantanen looks to continue his strong start to the season when the Dallas Stars visit the Pittsburgh Penguins on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Mikko Rantanen looks to continue his strong start to the season when the Dallas Stars visit the Pittsburgh Penguins on Saturday. Rantanen has six points in his past three games, including four points in a 4-0 road win over the Buffalo Sabres on Thursday. The Penguins will be playing the second contest of a back-to-back set and looking to snap a three-game losing streak (0-2-1) following a 3-2 shootout loss to the host Columbus Blue Jackets on Friday. A goal from Pittsburgh's Evgeni Malkin early in the third period tied it 2-2 and forced overtime. The Penguins had that opportunity because backup goalie Sergei Murashov stopped 43 shots. "He was awesome. Just really steady and made some big saves for us," Pittsburgh captain Sidney Crosby said about Murashov. "There were some extended shifts there where they controlled a lot of the play. I thought that he allowed ourselves to get organized a bit." Malkin notched his third goal of the season, but Crosby has just two points (both assists) through five games. Bryan Rust has provided a spark and scored his second goal in two games back from injury for the Penguins, who opened the season by scoring 13 goals in two games but have totaled seven in their past three. "I mean, the guys battled back to get that point," Penguins coach Dan Muse said, "but at the same time, I feel like we just left too much of that game on the table. You're going to walk away, good to get the point, but you're disappointed in the overall game and what I know we're capable of." Rantanen had a goal and three assists on Thursday as Dallas beat Buffalo for its second straight win. It was Rantanen's 26th career game with at least four points. Dallas' Jason Robertson, Sam Steel and Roope Hintz also scored, and Wyatt Johnston had three assists. "I just like the game all of our guys are giving us right now," Stars coach Glen Gulutzan said. "Our 'D' has been moving the puck great the last couple games, and our forwards are working to spots for them, so we're a little connected. We've just got to keep stacking here. We've got to stack plays and games up on each other." If Jake Oettinger starts in goal Saturday night, he would be looking for his third straight shutout. He made 26 saves against the Sabres to follow up on 13-save effort in a 5-0 win against the San Jose Sharks on Monday. "I thought (Thursday) we were even better than the last game," Gulutzan said. "I thought we were good against a really good hockey team." It is the second time in his career that Oettinger has posted back-to-back shutouts. His shutout streak is at 146:55, the second longest of his career behind a 154:20 stretch from March 28-April 7, 2024. Oettinger is 7-1-0 with a 1.87 goals-against average and a .932 save percentage versus the Penguins in his career. Pittsburgh's likely starter, Arturs Silovs, has never faced the Stars. The Stars took both games against the Penguins last season. Rantanen scored the shootout winner in a 3-2 game at Dallas last December, and the Stars prevailed 6-3 at Pittsburgh in March. --Field Level Media

item.title: The midterm strategy driving Democrats deep into Trump country
item.description: It may seem like overreach, but Democrats say they want to force Republicans to spend money defending safe seats, draining resources from swing districts that will decide control of the House.
item.dc:creator: Leah Douglas, Joseph Ax, Tim Reid
item.content:encoded: On paper, Democrat Justin Pearson, a 31-year-old Tennessee state legislator, has little chance of winning the state's 9th Congressional District, which Republican lawmakers redrew months ago from a Democratic stronghold to a deeply Republican seat. Yet this week the national Democratic Party added the rural district to its list of midterm targets in November, part of a broader strategy to compete in President Donald Trump's conservative heartland despite long odds of flipping it. On its face, the strategy may look like Democratic overreach. Voters living in the 9th District's newly reconfigured boundaries, for instance, picked Trump by more than 21 points in 2024. More than a dozen Democratic operatives, strategists and candidates told Reuters the goal in part is to force Republicans to spend money defending safe seats, draining resources from the swing districts that will decide control of the US House. By expanding the map, the party is also signaling to donors that races are becoming more competitive amid high prices and the Iran war driving Trump's unpopularity, helping unlock money that might otherwise stay on the sidelines, they said. "These expansions force Republicans to go on defense in more districts," said one House campaign official, speaking on the condition of anonymity. "It's also a signal to donors and outside groups that House Democrats are taking these races seriously." REPUBLICANS DISMISSIVE OF NEW MAP The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the party's US House campaign arm, this week added Pearson's race and 13 others to its target list, expanding its battlefield to 66 Republican-held seats. Getting on the target list gives candidates access to national party staff and campaign tools, while also raising their profiles with donors, potentially opening new streams of fundraising for their campaigns. There are early signs the strategy is having some effect. Republican-aligned groups have begun spending in some newly added districts, while two Democratic campaigns in Republican districts told Reuters their fundraising accelerated after being placed on the target list. Republicans have dismissed the idea that Democrats have a serious chance of defeating their party in districts that overwhelmingly voted for Trump in 2024. Mike Marinella, a spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee - the party's House campaign group - accused the Democratic Party of "stretching its map a mile wide and an inch deep, pretending every district in America is suddenly a battleground." He said the strategy will force Democrats to spend in long-shot contests when the party is already being outspent by Republicans. Analysts, too, are skeptical. "I'll take it seriously when they actually put their money where their mouth is. There is a point at which it becomes fantasy land," said David Wasserman, an elections analyst at the nonpartisan Cook Political Report, which rates many of these races as safely Republican. Democrats say they have chosen these districts for a number of reasons, including the quality of their candidates and the chance they might pull off upset wins to increase the size of a potential House majority. FOLLOWING THE MONEY It remains unclear how much money Democrats will ultimately devote to the newly added districts. Recent campaign finance filings are not yet available, and the party declined to tell Reuters where it is spending or how much it plans to spend on its expanded map. But there are signs Republicans are paying attention. Restoration of America PAC, funded primarily by billionaire Richard Uihlein, spent nearly $750,000 on digital ads backing Republican David Flippo in Nevada's 2nd District last week, according to Federal Election Commission filings. The district, which Trump carried by 14 points in 2024, is among the recent additions to the Democratic target list. "Democrats are on offense, Republicans are running scared, even in deep-red territory, and our expansive map reflects it," DCCC Chair Suzan DelBene said in a statement. The new target list includes districts in Arkansas, New York and Virginia that Trump carried by as many as 24 points. Democrats say rising costs and dissatisfaction with some Trump policies are creating openings in rural and Republican-leaning areas. "Rural America is unhappy with tariffs and rising fuel and farm costs, and that's pushing us into redder areas," Democratic pollster Celinda Lake said. Democrats will need a net gain of four to retake the House. However, only about 50 of the 435 House races are expected to be competitive. TENNESSEE DREAMING Tennessee Republicans in May split the heavily Democratic Memphis area into three districts, transforming the 9th from a majority-Black urban seat into a sprawling district stretching more than 200 miles (322 km) across rural western Tennessee, a change that made the seat significantly more favorable to Republicans. Yet Pearson says he has found independent and Republican voters frustrated by the high cost of living who are open to voting Democratic. "We've traveled across all 15 counties, filling churches and community centers in places people said we couldn't compete," said Pearson, a Black lawmaker who gained national attention in 2023 when the Republican-majority legislature expelled him for joining a gun-violence protest at the state Capitol. Republicans have portrayed Pearson as an outspoken progressive activist, pointing to his participation in gun-control and voting-rights protests. "The people in Tennessee Nine, they have a clear choice. They can choose confidence over chaos, and they can choose common sense over communism, and they can choose a lawmaker over a troublemaker," his Republican opponent, state senator Brent Taylor, told Reuters. There has been little public polling on the race, which Cook rates "Solid Republican." EXCITE DONORS Being added to the target list can quickly pay dividends for a campaign. Candidates or representatives from four Democratic campaigns on the DCCC's list told Reuters they either expected to see a boost in donations or were already seeing an uptick since their addition. Pearson said his campaign has seen a surge of financial support after being added to the list, which would boost his get-out-the-vote operation. "This race is going to be tight. It's going to be close. It's going to come down to how many people can we see before Election Day, knocking on those doors and reaching out to them directly," he said. But Democrats' ambitions are constrained by a relative cash shortage. While Democratic candidates nationally have outraised their Republican opponents, Republican national party committees and Republican-aligned super PACs have far outstripped Democratic counterparts in money raised. Democrats in tough races in the expanded map said they are connecting with small-dollar donors by focusing on cost-of-living issues and campaigning heavily at town halls and other local appearances.

item.title: The Week in Breakingviews: For whom the bell rings
item.description: As US stock markets set new records, this week’s update looks at some fresh cracks in the foundations of the artificial intelligence craze. Plus the threat to banks’ interest margins from AI agents, and Chinese car giant BYD’s attempt to follow Toyota’s global road.
item.dc:creator: Peter Thal Larsen
item.content:encoded: Welcome back! Governments across the West face rising bond yields. Will this trigger overdue tax reform and fiscal restraint, or a debt crisis? Let me know what you think. If this newsletter was forwarded to you, sign up here to get it in your inbox every weekend. OPENING LINE “Allison Kirkby is looking like Britain’s answer to Jamie Dimon. The BT (BT.L) CEO has just stepped in to buy up the carcass of indebted telecom group TalkTalk, just as the JPMorgan (JPM.N) boss is known for saving weak US banks.” Read more: [USN:L6N45R0MI TEXT:"BT’s vulture M&A dials up a worthwhile connection"] FIVE THINGS I LEARNED FROM BREAKINGVIEWS THIS WEEK Hiring a tanker to transit through the Strait of Hormuz to China now costs $1.2 million a day. ([USN:L6N45R0LH TEXT:"Tolls look more appealing"]) Discretionary government spending in Brazil accounts for less than 2% of GDP. ([USN:L6N45R0RL TEXT:"Little room for cuts"]) South Korea’s Samsung is set to make more profit than larger rival Nvidia this year. ([USN:L6N45U03L TEXT:"Valuations are very different"]) The price of jet fuel is double the average for last year. ([USN:L6N45L0U4 TEXT:"Trouble for engine specialists"]) Brewing giant AB InBev has launched a protein beer in Brazil. ([USN:L6N45R0VX TEXT:"But “proteinmaxxing” has limits"]) BURNING POINT When writing about financial markets, as when investing in them, timing is everything. By that yardstick, the cover story published by Barron’s in March 2000 can claim to be one of the best-timed works of financial journalism ever. Under the headline “ Burning Up ”, the article made the simple but devastating point that many hot internet startups of the era were using their financial resources so quickly they would run out of cash before the end of the year. It appeared 10 days after what turned out to be the peak of the dotcom bubble. Equity and debt markets dried up and valuations collapsed. It would be 15 years before the tech-focused Nasdaq Composite Index surpassed its previous peak. As the Nasdaq and S&P 500 benchmarks [USN:L6N45S0IV TEXT:"break records"] again this week, it is tempting to look at fresh cracks in the market’s foundations. There are plenty of contenders. Take Firmus Technologies, an Australian data centre operator backed by chip giant Nvidia (NVDA.O) and alternative asset manager Blackstone (BX.N) , which hoped to complete the country’s largest initial public offering in three decades. The so-called “neocloud” builds server farms and leases them to large tech companies. As Antony Currie [USN:L6N45S1EE TEXT:"explained"], executives touted a novel valuation measure – known as EV+1/EBIT+2 – to highlight its prospects. This unconventional ratio compares a company’s enterprise value – its market capitalisation plus net debt – in 12 months’ time to the earnings before interest and tax it expects to generate two years hence. The idea was to encourage investors to see hefty upfront investments in terms of their future payoff. It didn’t work. Firmus on Friday [USN:L6N45V00W TEXT:"cancelled its $31 billion listing"] citing “recent market volatility and prevailing market conditions.” Or take the news, reported by the Financial Times on Thursday, that OpenAI’s revenue was running at an annualised rate of about $50 billion in September – $20 billion less than the figure the FT and others had previously reported. The revelation is mainly a reminder that multiplying a company’s monthly revenue by 12 is a [USN:L6N3ZY167 TEXT:"crude and unreliable"] way of gauging its financial health. Nevertheless, it prompted an across-the-board selloff in listed tech stocks. These setbacks will not, on their own, prick the artificial intelligence bubble. Other data centre operators are making healthy returns on their investments in chips and energy: as Rob Cyran [USN:L6N45T0Y8 TEXT:"points out"], SpaceX’s (SPCX.O) chief financial officer says Elon Musk’s company should earn back its initial outlay in less than a year. Meanwhile, OpenAI’s mooted trillion-dollar-plus valuation depends less on how much revenue it brought in last month than what it might be generating in two or three years’ time. Shareholders also have a habit of freaking out prematurely. Recall the brief selloff triggered by the release of Chinese startup DeepSeek’s new AI model in early 2025. Still, investors are increasingly jittery. The yield on 10-year US government debt – the main reference point for global borrowing costs – has risen by around a percentage point since late April, changing the calculus for debt-heavy projects. Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO, which is supposed to take place before the end of November , will be a [USN:L6N45F0XJ TEXT:"test of confidence"]. Only with hindsight, though, will we be able to point to the article that marked the top of the current frenzy. CHART OF THE WEEK When code-writing artificial intelligence bots tanked software stocks, investors dubbed it the SaaSpocalypse. Now banks are in the firing line. The arrival of digital assistants like Meta Platforms’ (META.O) Muse could help complacent consumers earn higher interest rates on deposits, squeezing the net interest margin (NIM) banks make on the spread with loan charges. Stephen Gandel [USN:L6N45N19E TEXT:"crunched the numbers"] on the $3.8 trillion currently stashed in US savings accounts. Raising the rate from the current 1.9% to 4% would cost those lenders a hefty $79 billion a year in lost income. Get ready for the NIMageddon. THE WEEK IN PODCASTS The revelation that Manchester City benefited from sham contracts worth $1.1 billion over almost a decade has roiled English soccer. It also has far-reaching business and financial implications (See [USN:L6N45O0WL TEXT:"Britain’s soccer sham"]). Liam Proud and Jon Sindreu joined Jonathan Guilford in the Viewsroom to debate whether it’s possible to design a level playing field when the financial stakes are so high, and what the scandal means for investors rushing to buy big sports teams. The notion that stocks and bonds follow a rational path has been widely debunked. But are idiosyncrasies becoming more visible? On The Big View I talked to Alex Edmans, the academic and author of “The Madness of Markets”, about whether the rules of investing have changed. PARTING SHOT Toyota rose from being a Japanese upstart to become the world’s largest carmaker. So it’s tempting to imagine whether BYD, the Chinese electric vehicle juggernaut, can follow the same route. Indeed, founder Wang Chuanfu says he aims to become the biggest manufacturer of automobiles on the planet by 2030, which would mean overtaking Toyota. Yet as Katrina Hamlin [USN:L6N45K0H1 TEXT:"writes"], the road for BYD is a lot bumpier and narrower than the one followed by its Japanese rival. The Chinese company must overcome stagnating sales, export barriers, hostile governments overseas, and cut-throat competition at home. Toyota has shown the way, but BYD will have to drive even faster to match it. Want to receive The Week in Breakingviews in your inbox every Saturday? Sign up for the newsletter here . Follow Peter Thal Larsen on Bluesky and LinkedIn .

item.title: Hastings like a local
item.description: Our desk editor’s guide to castle views, shipwrecks and seasonal festivals.
item.dc:creator: Alexandra Hudson
item.content:encoded: REUTERS/Illustration/Kate Evans Famous for the eponymous battle of 1066 that inspired the Bayeux Tapestry , the British seaside town of Hastings — my home of the last decade — has a thriving cultural life, magnificent natural setting and rough-around-the-edges charm that grows on you quickly. The beach is the star attraction, atmospheric pubs and cafes abound, and of course there are Hastings' evocative historical sites — not least the ruined Hastings Castle , constructed by William, Duke of Normandy, after winning the English throne. I grew up in Brighton, also on the country's southern coast, and settled in Hastings with my family after postings in Berlin, Amsterdam, and Istanbul for Reuters. The sea air and screeching seagulls made it quickly feel like home. Hastings is not immune to the problems affecting Britain's coastal towns, including a lack of employment and some deprivation, and it has seen its fortunes rise and fall over the decades. But the town is drawing more visitors and blossoming with fresh energy and new ventures. Here is how to visit Hastings like a local: Getting around: Hastings and neighbouring St Leonards-on-Sea, once a Regency-era resort and now the edgier of the two, form one urban area that is best explored on foot. Walking from central St Leonards to Hastings along the seafront promenade takes less than one hour. The elegant apartment blocks give way to British seaside staples like mini golf, go-karts and amusement arcades before you reach the Old Town, with its compact streets of timbered houses. People relax at Goat Ledge beach cafe at St Leonards-on-Sea, next to Hastings, Britain, October 4, 2026. REUTERS/Toby Melville People relax at a cafe on West Hill in Hastings Old Town, Hastings, Britain, October 4, 2026. REUTERS/Toby Melville A person views Hastings Old Town and Hastings beach as they travel on the funicular railway on East Hill. REUTERS/Toby Melville A view of Battle Abbey, built on the site of the Battle of Hastings in 1066, in Battle. REUTERS/Toby Melville If arriving by train, alight at St Leonards Warrior Square station and walk down Kings Road, a vibrant street of cafes, second-hand bookshops, vintage furniture stores and artist-run outlets selling bold screenprints and ceramics. It holds a street market on the first Saturday of each month, featuring handicrafts, organic food, and jewellery. Turn left at the end of the road for your first glimpse of the sea. What to see: One of my favourite spots on the beach is the strip along Warrior Square and Bottle Alley, a split-level promenade. Beachfront cafes such as Goat Ledge , Starsky & Hatch and The Selkie have breathed new life into this area, and it is a popular place to bask in the sun with a coffee or lunch. The brightly painted wooden huts, twinkly lights and bistro tables on the pebbles bring a festival vibe and you’ll often hear live music here. A short walk further along the seafront brings you to George Street, a charming pedestrian lane of restaurants, pubs and gift shops at the foot of the castle. The West Hill lift is a historic Victorian funicular railway that will transport you up to the Norman castle for £5.50 ($7.40) round-trip. There you’ll find magnificent views across the English Channel towards France, as well as yoga classes and outdoor film screenings. The West Hill is also home to the Smugglers Adventure , a fun attraction that tells stories of piracy and smuggling in a warren of caves reputedly once used to conceal contraband. In the 1960s, the caves housed a subterranean nightclub. To return to the Old Town, hop back on the funicular or follow one of the several steep, winding paths. Look out for the twittens — narrow, medieval alleyways between the houses, as you weave through All Saints Street, Tackleway and the High Street. What to eat: If you fancy seafood, the grilled “catch of the day” fish bap (or sandwich) at Goat Ledge is always delicious. Alternatively, pick up traditional fish and chips and eat them on the beach. Just watch out for diving seagulls going for your chips. People relax at Goat Ledge beach cafe at St Leonards-on-Sea. REUTERS/Toby Melville People relax at Selkie Seafood Bar at St Leonards-on-Sea. REUTERS/Toby Melville Oyster shells and other sea food are seen on a beachside table at Selkie Seafood Bar at St Leonards-on-Sea. REUTERS/Toby Melville In St Leonards, Half Man! Half Burger! has some of the best burgers — meat and vegetarian — I've ever tasted, and Three Faces has incredible tapas. Culture fix: Hastings is unusual in having a beach-launched fishing fleet, with the boats hauled back on to the pebbles when not in use. Right beside them is Hastings Contemporary , a wonderful art gallery whose design mirrors that of the historic black Net Shops used for stowing fishing equipment. A fisherman throws equipment from a boat after returning from a fishing trip in The Stade area of Hastings Old Town. Hastings has one of the largest working beach-launched fishing fleets in Europe. REUTERS/Toby Melville A tractor pulls a fishing boat up the beach in The Stade area of Hastings Old Town. REUTERS/Toby Melville Walk along Rock-a-Nore Road and stop at the excellent (and free) Fishermen's Museum , which highlights the history of the fleet and tragic storms that have struck. Opposite is the 1902 East Hill lift, Britain's steepest funicular, which takes you up to Hastings Country Park — a beautiful expanse of rolling sandstone cliffs, with breathtaking views down to the sea. Look out for the roaming ponies that graze the heathland. A young person views exhibits at the Fishermen's Museum in Hastings Old Town. REUTERS/Toby Melville For music lovers, Hastings Philharmonic runs excellent classical concerts throughout the year. Check the tides: Hastings has a pebble beach, but at low tide, vast stretches of sand are exposed, offering ample space for long strolls. I like to time sea swims for high tide and beach walks for low tide. If this falls at sunset, you'll find the beach packed with locals savouring the views. Look out for hagstones, pebbles with natural holes. A few times a year, when the tide falls below 60 cm (2 feet), you can glimpse the wreck of the Amsterdam, a Dutch East India Company ship that ran aground in 1749 outside St Leonards and was exposed by shifting sands in 1969. It makes for an eerie sight. A replica is moored outside Amsterdam's Maritime Museum , while Hastings' excellent Shipwreck Museum displays the bottles, spoons and other goods found onboard. The 1066 battlefield: A 15-minute train ride 6 miles (9.5 km) inland brings you to the town of Battle, where King Harold’s Saxon army was defeated by William’s Norman invaders. You can visit the former battlefield and ruined abbey, built by William's son on the spot where Harold perished, and explore a medieval gatehouse. Centuries on, walking the trail around the battlefield where thousands died remains a sombre and moving experience. A good pint: Hastings has no shortage of charming local boozers. The 16th-century Stag Inn on All Saints Street has a pretty, tiered garden overlooking the rooftops. Look out for the mummified cat that was found encased within the chimney — a practice said to ward off evil in British folklore. Another good pub is the FILO (First In Last Out) on the High Street, with an unusual indoor fire pit and cosy wooden booths that are always packed on weekends. It brews its own traditional ales and has been joined in recent years by other craft beer makers, including The Brewing Brothers , who run three excellent venues. In the Old Town, the Jenny Lind , named after a 19th-century Swedish opera singer, is one of Hastings' most-loved pubs with regular acoustic nights and folk, rock and sea shanty sessions. Over in St Leonards, The Piper draws a younger crowd and holds regular gigs upstairs. Get festive: Dig out green clothes and flower crowns for the annual "Jack in the Green" folk festival on the first Monday of May. Dancers and drummers dressed in green parade through the town and up on to the West Hill, where the Jack — a crowned figure clad in foliage — is symbolically slain to release the spirit of summer. It's all rather reminiscent of the 1973 folk horror film "The Wicker Man," and seems to get bigger every year. A participant attends the annual May Day bank holiday Jack In The Green parade and festival. REUTERS/Toby Melville Participants attend the annual May Day bank holiday Jack In The Green parade and festival. REUTERS/Toby Melville A participant attends the annual May Day bank holiday Jack In The Green parade and festival. REUTERS/Toby Melville In July, locals rustle up striped shirts and eye patches for Pirate Weekend , which brings three days of live music to the shore, and a noisy parade through the town for all “pirates” to join. In October, an annual bonfire marks the anniversary of the Norman Conquest, with a flaming torch procession through the Old Town and a huge blaze and fireworks on the beach. For £3.90 ($5.17), you can get a scoop of gelato at Di Pola's . Great place to see a sunset: The coastal paths of the Country Park, or the West or East Hill

item.title: Record-breaking Renshaw puts Australia on top in Durban
item.description: Matt Renshaw struck a career-best 190 to guide Australia to 390 all out on day two of the first test against South Africa at Kingsmead on Saturday, as the home side reached 27 for one in reply before play was ended prematurely by bad light.
item.dc:creator: Mark Gleeson
item.content:encoded: Matt Renshaw struck a career-best 190 to guide Australia to 390 all out on day two of the first test against South Africa at Kingsmead on Saturday, as the home side reached 27 for one in reply before play was ended prematurely by bad light. Aiden Markram (15 not out) and David Bedingham (12 not out) will resume on the third morning for South Africa, who were frustrated by the record-breaking innings of Renshaw. Ryan Rickelton was the hosts' wicket to fall when he was caught at third slip by Beau Webster for a duck off the bowling of Josh Hazlewood. The day belonged to Renshaw as he shared a record ninth-wicket stand of 134 for Australia against South Africa with Nathan Lyon (27), also the highest partnership for that wicket in Durban. "There was a lot of thinking today while batting," Renshaw said. "How many balls can I face? How do I get off strike when I need to? It was thinking what we can try and do, trying to find the right options, find a boundary if we could. "Keeping them out in the field, getting their quicks coming back on. I saw (Marco) Jansen bowled 30-odd (overs), (Anrich) Nortje 30-odd, so they've got some overs into the frontline bowlers in the first innings of the first game." His score is the highest by a number five batter in tests at Kingsmead, but he was out soon after tea when he edged spinner Simon Harmer to Markram at slip. Australia were in trouble early in Renshaw's innings as they slipped to 124 for six on day one. EARLY TROUBLE But Renshaw flipped the script after putting on 86 for the seventh wicket with skipper Pat Cummins (43). Australia started the second day on 187 for six and frustrated the home side before Wiaan Mulder (4-68) had Cummins caught by Markram at second slip. Mitchell Starc (6) followed quickly after being bowled by Mulder, and at it looked as though South Africa would run through the lower order. Lyon was circumspect, however, and Renshaw rotated the strike superbly to make sure he had most of the strike and continued to accumulate runs rather than attack the bowling. Lyon fell LBW to Marco Jansen (3-68). Renshaw’s 190 has come off 397 balls, a classic test innings of patience and waiting for the bad ball. He was struck in the helmet by speedster Anrich Nortje, but he soon settled again and his second test century came nine years after his first, 185 against Pakistan in 2017. Renshaw had made single-figure scores in 11 of his previous 13 test innings. "He played beautifully throughout the innings, played what was in front of him and left well," Mulder said. "The partnerships built around him and he played the situation as well as anyone could have at this level. "It is a good cricket wicket and will get a bit up and down as the game goes on and spin more."

item.title: Rosatom and Finland's Fennovoima claim different wins after tribunal ruling
item.description: Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom and Finnish utility Fennovoima each highlighted different parts of an International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) tribunal ruling as favourable on Saturday, in a long-running dispute over the cancelled Hanhikivi-1 nuclear power project.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom and Finnish utility Fennovoima each highlighted different parts of an International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) tribunal ruling as favourable on Saturday, in a long-running dispute over the cancelled Hanhikivi-1 nuclear power project. The parties have been locked in legal disputes since Fennovoima scrapped the 7-billion-euro ($7.8 billion) project in May 2022, citing significant delays and political risks shortly after Russia launched its conflict in Ukraine . Rosatom said the tribunal found that Fennovoima had unlawfully terminated the contract for the construction of the planned plant in northern Finland. "Today's victory is important, but not final. We will continue to prove that we are right regarding the Finnish project in courts of various instances," Rosatom Director General Alexey Likhachev said in a statement, which did not refer to any financial outcome. Fennovoima said the tribunal found that it had not been entitled to terminate the contract, but that it was entitled to receive reimbursements of advance payments and interest in excess of 1 billion euros ($1.12 billion). It said the tribunal offset both sides' claims, resulting in Rosatom subsidiaries being ordered to pay Fennovoima a net 606 million euros plus interest. The ICC did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The contract to build the 1.2 gigawatt plant was signed in 2013 with Fennovoima, a consortium in which Finnish stakeholders including Fortum, Outokumpu and SSAB originally controlled two thirds through a joint venture, and the Russian side held one third. After the project's termination, Fennovoima wound down its operations and is primarily engaged in legal proceedings. ($1 = 0.8928 euros)

item.title: Singapore sprint underway after rain delay
item.description: The start of the Singapore Grand Prix sprint race on Saturday was delayed by half an hour due to heavy rain at the Marina Bay Street Circuit.
item.dc:creator: Rohith Nair
item.content:encoded: The start of the Singapore Grand Prix sprint race on Saturday was delayed by half an hour due to heavy rain at the Marina Bay Street Circuit. A shower minutes before the scheduled 5 p.m. (0900 GMT) start sent fans and officials rushing for cover while standing water around turns 2 and 3 forced the FIA to put back the start after the medical car had assessed track conditions. Once the standing water was cleared, the FIA said drivers would do two formation laps behind the safety car as teams quickly swapped out the slick tyres for intermediates. "The spray is very bad," McLaren's Oscar Piastri said on the team radio as the drivers did two formation laps before a standing start for the final sprint race of the season. Red Bull's Max Verstappen took [USN:L1N45V0HG TEXT:"pole position for the sprint"] ahead of Mercedes driver George Russell and Ferrari's Charles Leclerc. Last weekend, the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia descended into chaos as heavy rain at the Sepang circuit triggered [USN:L1N45Q01D TEXT:"multiple delays and a suspended start procedure"] that left drivers scrambling in treacherous conditions.

item.title: Thailand prepares to host IMF-World Bank meetings
item.description: Thailand is preparing to host the IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok from October 12–18, bringing together more than 15,000 participants from 191 countries, including central bank governors, economic policymakers and business leaders, for discussions on the world economy.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Thailand is preparing to host the IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok from October 12–18, bringing together more than 15,000 participants from 191 countries, including central bank governors, economic policymakers and business leaders, for discussions on the world economy. To ease traffic, Bangkok government offices will work from home on October 12, 14 and 15, while October 13 is an existing public holiday and October 16 has been declared a special government and bank holiday, with private companies and state enterprises asked to consider suitable arrangements. Security has been tightened at the meeting venue in central Bangkok and 21 official hotels, according to the authorities. About 500 Tourist Police officers will also help secure the venue, delegate hotels and tourist attractions through undercover deployments, patrols, drones and motorcade escorts coordinated with around 39 embassies, Tourist Police Bureau Commissioner Phongsiam Meekhanthong said. Visiting leaders include Swiss President Guy Parmelin, making the first official visit to Thailand by a Swiss president in 22 years, and Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, the Thai Foreign Ministry said. Participants’ spending could generate 1.05–2.25 billion baht for the Thai economy, according to the Thai Finance Ministry. More than 320 electric vehicles will serve participants to cut carbon emissions, the Thai Finance Ministry said. Heavy to very heavy rain is forecast for Bangkok and surrounding provinces on October 10–11, potentially causing localised flooding, the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration warned. This comes after parts of the city [USN:L6N45I012 TEXT:"flooded"] two weeks ago following 320 mm (12.6 inches) of rain over three days.

item.title: All Blacks crush Australia with second-half blitz to retain Bledisloe Cup
item.description: Australia's hopes of wresting back the Bledisloe Cup for the first time in a generation were crushed in familiar fashion in a comprehensive 50-19 loss to New Zealand at Auckland's Eden Park on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Australia's hopes of wresting back the Bledisloe Cup for the first time in a generation were crushed in familiar fashion in a comprehensive 50-19 loss to New Zealand at Auckland's Eden Park on Saturday. The Wallabies were in touch at 17-14 down at halftime but the All Blacks scored five tries after the break to ensure they will retain the symbol of trans-Tasman Sea supremacy for a 24th straight year ahead of next week's second test in Sydney. Tries from Peter Lakai, Tupou Vaa'i, Cam Roigard, skipper Codie Taylor, Leroy Carter, Josh Moorby and Will Jordan combined with 15 points from the boot of flyhalf Damian McKenzie got the All Blacks back to winning ways after three straight losses to South Africa. "We were hurting a little bit after the (South Africa series), but it's awesome to come home, play in front of our fans, our people. We've missed it, and to get a result like that, it's hugely proud of the boys," said Taylor, whose try helped New Zealand extend their unbeaten run at Eden Park to 54 matches since 1994. "This is home for us ... You see ex-All Blacks standing on the sidelines. You want to do it for those men, the people that have been before you, and you just want to continue the legacy." Australia, who came into the game unbeaten in six matches and looking for a first win at Eden Park since 1986, scored first-half tries through fullback Tom Wright and captain Harry Wilson and earned a late consolation score from hooker Josh Nasser. “Playing them here, it's always going to be tough and we did a really good job to be in the fight after that first half,” said Wilson. “We fought back really well and then we had an opportunity at the start of the second half and we blew it, and then it was tough to get the ball back for the next 30 minutes.” The Wallabies, buoyed by a win over world champions South Africa last month, dominated the opening exchanges and got their reward in the eighth minute when fullback Wright cleverly straightened up an attacking move to score the opening try. The aerial battle was always going to be a key factor and New Zealand were enjoying the better of it with Jordie Barrett winning one duel and feeding McKenzie, who scythed through the defence before feeding flanker Lakai to level up the scores. The All Blacks were also getting a width in the attack that was causing Australia problems and the home side cashed in to take a 14-7 lead in the 16th minute, when Vaa'i barrelled low and hard through the defence at the end of a multi-phase attack. Ryan Lonergan missed a kickable penalty for Australia in the 24th minute, but McKenzie made no mistake from closer range nine minutes later to extend the lead to 10 points. The five minutes before halftime is traditionally a fruitful stage of the game for New Zealand, but it was Australia who scored three minutes before the break, with Ben Donaldson scooting through a gap in the defence and finding Wilson in support. Australia again came firing out of the blocks in the second half but New Zealand earned the first points after 50 minutes when scrumhalf Roigard darted over the line off the back of a rolling maul to extend their lead to 24-14. The All Blacks were now relentless in attack and hooker Taylor, captaining the side for the second time, scored their fourth try five minutes later. The Wallabies were now struggling to hold onto the ball and wingers Carter, Moorby and Jordan capitalised on the remorseless pressure from the All Blacks in the last quarter to put the game well beyond the visitors.

item.title: From 'cockroach' post to protest leader: India's Dipke tests Modi government
item.description: His six-word reply to the Supreme Court's chief justice shot him to fame.
item.dc:creator: Tora Agarwala
item.content:encoded: Indian police detained on Saturday Abhijeet Dipke, the political strategist who turned a "cockroach" jibe at unemployed youth into a nationwide protest movement that helped force the resignation of a federal minister. Police met Dipke's aircraft as it landed in the capital of New Delhi ahead of a rally demanding the resignation of the election chief over accusations of [USN:L4N45K0E7 TEXT:"voter list manipulation"] that critics say dropped about 130 million voters from a draft roll. "I have come to be arrested, arrest me ... I am not afraid of you guys," Dipke told police officers aboard the aircraft, in television images that showed one of them assuring him he was not being arrested, but rather that his cooperation was sought. Dipke, 31, born in a Dalit family on the lower rungs of India's caste system, shot to fame this year after his six-word response to Supreme Court Chief Justice Surya Kant's remarks likening unemployed youth to "cockroaches" went viral online. The post spawned the satirical "Cockroach Janta Party", an online movement that rapidly evolved into a political force. It mobilised mass street protests that culminated in the July resignation of education minister Dharmendra Pradhan, a rare exit from Prime Minister Narendra Modi's cabinet, following sustained public pressure. Dipke's detention came after he called for a [USN:L1N45W00K TEXT:"fresh protest"] on Saturday seeking the resignation of election commission chief [USN:L4N45K0DB TEXT:"Gyanesh Kumar"] over the changes. The election panel says the figure, which is larger than the population of Japan, comprises entries flagged during draft revision, and that voters wrongly removed can enroll again. Bearded and usually wearing T-shirt and jeans, Dipke had led a protest in the southern tech hub of Bengaluru before travelling via Mumbai to the capital, where police detained him with two senior group leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka. Despite a police crackdown in Delhi and tight protest restrictions, Dipke urged supporters to demonstrate peacefully, citing the example of Mahatma Gandhi, India's apostle of non-violence. "I don't know what will happen tomorrow," Dipke said in a video recorded before Saturday's flight. "But one thing I am sure of is that I am not going to be afraid. Neither am I going to step back. We have to save our democracy." Authorities called in thousands of security forces to fortify Delhi, with travel and telecoms links suspended, in a [USN:L1N45W00K TEXT:"lockdown"] designed to stop the youth protest. "Why is the prime minister so scared of the country's youth, the country's people?" Dipke asked before his flight. UNLIKELY EVENTS SET OFF BY SIX-WORD POST "What if all cockroaches come together?" was Dipke's question in a May social media post that almost overnight turned the political communications professional into one of the most recognisable faces of India's youth protest movement. He returned to India after completing a master's degree in public relations in the United States, saying his viral success had given him "a chance to do actual, meaningful work", despite threats he and his family received. The "Cockroach Janta Party" amassed millions of followers online and helped drive protests over leaks of a medical entrance examination paper affecting about 2 million candidates. The movement eventually focused its anger on Pradhan, who resigned on July 25. Since then, Dipke and his supporters, who see the group as a political pressure movement rather than a party, have campaigned on issues ranging from government school infrastructure to jobs for young people. It returned to the streets after a report last month in the Indian Express newspaper. The paper said two of election chief Kumar's deputies had repeatedly raised concerns about voter-roll revisions, registration procedures and the commission's digital systems. The poll body has said differing views are normal during internal deliberations. (This story has been corrected to fix the spelling of Abhijeet Dipke's first name in paragraph 1.)

item.title: Marquez takes championship lead with Indonesian GP sprint win
item.description: Ducati's Marc Marquez seized the lead in the championship standings for the first time in 2026 on Saturday by winning a dramatic Indonesian MotoGP sprint, after title rival Jorge Martin's race unravelled amid tyre issues.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Ducati's Marc Marquez seized the lead in the championship standings for the first time in 2026 on Saturday by winning a dramatic Indonesian MotoGP sprint, after title rival Jorge Martin's race unravelled amid tyre issues. Marquez's eighth sprint victory of the campaign moved him to 343 points, four ahead of Martin, completing a remarkable comeback for the defending champion, who trailed then-series leader Marco Bezzecchi by 102 points after the Italian Grand Prix in May. "It was a very tough race, especially from the beginning, and then when I saw that Martin was leading, I pushed with all I have," said Marquez, who was left exhausted by the hot and humid conditions. In a chaotic start to the sprint, [USN:L4N45W00O TEXT:"polesitter Raul Fernandez"] and Bezzecchi found themselves lying in the gravel after the first turn, while Aprilia's Martin surged into the lead from the second row, with Marquez hot on his heels. Martin quickly stretched his advantage and appeared headed for victory before deliberately conceding the lead to Marquez with five laps remaining to avoid a tyre-pressure penalty. The 2024 MotoGP champion did his best to retake the lead from Marquez, but ran wide in his dogged pursuit and ultimately failed to finish on the podium, coming in fourth. Trackhouse rider Ai Ogura was second, with Fabio Di Giannantonio (VR46 Racing) taking a third-placed finish on his birthday. "I did a big mistake on the third lap, fourth lap, and then he opened a gap," Marquez said. "In the last part of the race, I was able to catch him, I think he had some problem with the tyre pressure. "In the end, I felt better and better with the laps, my pace was better, but in the end, as always, I tried to manage the risk. These 12 points in the Mandalika sprint race are super important." The victory also appeared to end Marquez's run of misfortune in Indonesia. The Spaniard has endured a torrid record at Mandalika and suffered a season-ending collarbone injury there last year. On Sunday, the 33-year-old will be hoping to complete his first-ever full MotoGP race at the Mandalika circuit after a string of crashes and technical setbacks in previous appearances.

item.title: Barrier ready to make history in Route du Rhum on ocean-racing giant
item.description: Alexia Barrier looks impossibly small at the helm of IDEC Sport-CIC, a 32-metre (105-foot) trimaran capable of hurtling across the ocean at more than 40 knots. Soon, she will be entirely alone.
item.dc:creator: Vincent Daheron
item.content:encoded: Alexia Barrier looks impossibly small at the helm of IDEC Sport-CIC, a 32-metre (105-foot) trimaran capable of hurtling across the ocean at more than 40 knots. Soon, she will be entirely alone. On November 1, the 46-year-old French sailor will climb aboard the giant vessel in Saint-Malo and attempt something no woman has done before: race solo in the giant ULTIM class in the Route du Rhum. “It’s the biggest machine participating in offshore sailing around the world,” Barrier told Reuters. “Only eight of this kind are on the planet. So I’m happy, proud and privileged to be skipper of this machine.” On a bright October morning in Brest, Barrier looked tiny on the deck of the huge red trimaran, 23 metres (75 feet) wide with a mast towering 34 metres (112 feet) above the water. She hoisted the mainsail to the sound of the Black Eyed Peas’ “Meet Me Halfway”, rehearsing the manoeuvres she will soon have to perform entirely alone. Even in the light breeze, the boat quickly accelerated towards 23 knots. “The sails are huge. It’s really powerful. A sail is more than 100 kilos. I’m 55 kilos,” she said. “It goes so fast and if you make a mistake, it can be terrible because you can hurt the boat and hurt yourself. I’m super happy, but I’m more focused than ever.” The boat has reached speeds of around 46 knots. Barrier laughs about the prospect of matching that herself. “The record is about 46 knots, but you have to be a bit crazy to be at the helm at that speed,” she joked. FIRST ALL-FEMALE CREW Nine months ago, Barrier was leading the first all-female crew to set a reference time for the Jules Verne Trophy, sailing non-stop around the world. Now she is swapping that camaraderie for the peculiar solitude of single-handed ocean racing. “When I came back from the Jules Verne Trophy, for me it was obvious,” she said of taking on the Route du Rhum alone. “It feels like it was in another life when I’m sailing solo. I miss my crewmates. Sometimes I catch myself looking around, searching for one of them at her usual station and she’s not there.” Music will be one companion. Barrier is still working on the playlist that will soundtrack roughly a week alone at sea. But there will be little time for distraction aboard a machine where the combination of enormous power, speed and physical demands means a small error can quickly become a serious one. Barrier knows, too, that this voyage is about more than a finishing position. One of only 13 women to have completed the Vendee Globe, and now the skipper who led the all-female Jules Verne attempt, she has become accustomed to being the first woman through doors that have traditionally been difficult to open. “It’s part of my career. I’ve been racing for 20 years now, and it’s my life. For me, it’s a new step,” she said. “In a way, it’s cool to be the first. I can open a path for other women or little girls that are still wondering: ‘Shall I try, shall I do it?’” 'ELITE OF SAILING' Breaking into ULTIM racing required Barrier to find not only the experience but the money and team needed to operate at what she calls “the elite of sailing”. Even now she can scarcely believe where that journey has taken her. Standing on the dock in Brest, Barrier recalled thinking of the challenge ahead: “I dreamed too big.” Then she smiled. Because with the Route du Rhum approaching, the dream has become very real. Barrier, naturally, is already dreaming a little bigger. “In my dreams, if the magic happens, reaching the podium would be amazing,” she said. “It’s also important to allow yourself to dream big.” Nobody knows that better than Barrier.

item.title: Russian attack on Ukrainian city kills 20, a day after Trump eases diesel sanctions on Moscow
item.description: The strike on Zaporizhzhia, which killed three children, came a day after President Trump announced a deal to lift sanctions on Russian diesel.
item.dc:creator: Sergiy Chalyi, Max Hunder
item.content:encoded: Twenty people, including three children, were killed in a Russian attack on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia on Saturday, a day after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to lift sanctions on Russian diesel in a major setback for Kyiv. "Today, Russia said thank you for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said, in some of his sharpest criticism yet of the White House. Zaporizhzhia has been a regular target of Russian bombardment with strikes [USN:L8N43Z01W TEXT:"intensifying in the past few months."] A 6-year-old girl was among those killed when one strike reduced part of an apartment block to rubble. Her grandfather, Anatoliy Chumniy, stood sobbing over her body, laid on the ground in a white bag, after rescuers pulled it from the wreckage. "Her birthday would have been at the end of the month," he said through tears. Eighteen others were wounded in the attack on the industrial city, with a pre-war population of over 700,000 and whose outskirts lie less than 30 km (20 miles) from the front line. RUSSIA ESCALATING ATTACKS ON UKRAINIAN CITIES It was the third mass-casualty attack on Ukraine this week. Nearly 80 civilians were killed in Russian strikes on Wednesday and Thursday, including at least 30 killed by a bomb in the eastern garrison city of Kramatorsk and 22 others by a missile in the town of Pryluky, 80 miles east of Kyiv. A senior official in Zaporizhzhia, Mykhailo Semikin, said Russia had hit several locations simultaneously in the early hours of Saturday. Rescuers clambered through crumbled masonry to pull other residents of the building out alive. One man, whose leg was trapped in the rubble, screamed in pain as he was being freed. "If (the Russians) have money, they’ll be able to carry on fighting us," said Nataliia Malysheva, a 49-year-old local resident whose parents died in hospital after being pulled from the rubble. "How many lives have been lost here, how many homes have been destroyed? How many innocent people have died in the meantime?" MOSCOW NEEDS 'DIFFERENT SIGNALS' "Last night provided yet more confirmation that Russia perceives any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly keep fighting, that it can supposedly keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed," Zelenskiy said. A missile attack on Saturday afternoon also hit a restaurant, wounding seven people in Kyiv. Russian drones flew over Kyiv throughout the day, part of a vast new wave of bombardment of the capital, the heaviest since the early days of the war. Russia’s Defence Ministry said on Saturday its drones had struck a data-processing centre in Kyiv and a cargo ship carrying military supplies to the Ukrainian port of Odesa. TRUMP LIFTS DIESEL SANCTIONS Trump's decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports comes as his administration seeks to curb fuel prices, which have risen sharply during the US conflict with Iran . Kyiv had instead urged Washington to increase pressure on Moscow in an effort to force it into serious negotiations to end the four-and-a-half-year war . Trump, meanwhile, has criticised Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he claims have driven up global prices. Kyiv has said it wants a total halt on all energy strikes by both sides as Moscow pummels Ukraine's power grid. On Saturday, parts of Kyiv and the surrounding region were left without power, bringing the city's metro trains to a complete halt for the second time this week. The latest strikes came after Ukrainian and European officials held talks with US negotiators in Miami on Friday aimed at developing a common proposal for ending the war, according to [USN:FWN45V1JO TEXT:"a person familiar with the discussions"]. Trump announced the diesel deal while the negotiations were underway, a move Zelenskiy said had caught Kyiv by surprise. The Ukrainian delegation was headed home on Saturday, presidential aide Dmytro Lytvyn was cited by the Interfax Ukraine news agency as saying. Russian President Vladimir Putin said after a call with Trump that an immediate resumption of peace talks was unlikely, citing Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow. US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner may visit Moscow within the next two weeks, Russian state news agency TASS reported on Saturday, citing a source. Four civilians were killed and five others were wounded as a result of Ukrainian attacks on the [USN:S8N42201C TEXT:"Russian-controlled Luhansk region"] in eastern Ukraine, the Russian-installed governor said on Saturday. Reuters could not independently verify the report and there was no immediate comment from Ukraine.

item.title: French policing under scrutiny as student protest injuries mount
item.description: Fourteen-year-old Eden suffered a broken jaw and multiple smashed teeth when he was struck by a tear gas canister directed towards him at close range by a police officer last week during student protests in France, his parents and family lawyer said.
item.dc:creator: Juliette Jabkhiro, Layli Foroudi
item.content:encoded: Fourteen-year-old Eden suffered a broken jaw and multiple smashed teeth when he was struck by a tear gas canister directed towards him at close range by a police officer last week during student protests in France, his parents and family lawyer said. The teenager had been sitting on a wall looking at his phone metres away from the protest in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumone, the lawyer said. An officer approached him and struck him with a baton, prompting Eden to respond with a kick, according to the local prosecutor. A second officer then fired a tear gas grenade with a Cougar launcher, hitting him in the face. "(The officer) shot him in the mouth and left him lying on the ground, without even calling the emergency services," said lawyer Elsa Marcel. The family, who asked for Eden's second name to be withheld to protect their privacy, has filed a complaint for attempted murder, she said. A police spokesperson said they do not comment on ongoing investigations. The prosecutor's office said in a statement that the student had confronted the police and the officers tried to push him back. The officer was placed under formal investigation on charges of assault by a public official resulting in permanent disability or disfigurement on Tuesday, eight days after the incident. The case is one of 24 under investigation by the IGPN internal police watchdog linked to the policing of a more-than-two-week-long wave of [USN:L8N45S08G TEXT:"student unrest"] over [USN:L6N45M1EJ TEXT:"conditions"] in schools. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has described the demonstrations as the most violent in decades. The police response has renewed calls for the withdrawal of the use of rubber bullets and grenade launchers, which are not used by police in many other European countries and have been repeatedly criticised in recent years by rights groups, including Amnesty International and UN human rights experts, as dangerous and disproportionate. It has also sparked anger among the public and fanned support for a protest movement that is the latest manifestation of deep-seated [USN:L8N45L0FB TEXT:"discontent"] with President Emmanuel Macron’s government ahead of a 2027 election. Via interviews and reviews of legal documents, Reuters has documented 28 cases of injuries suffered due to police force, of which 15 are among those under investigation by the IGPN. They involve the use of rubber bullets, stun grenades, tear gas, batons and charges on horseback. In two cases, a person's eye has been lost or injured due to rubber bullets. In another, a 15-year-old in Lens had his hand blown off — likely by a stun grenade, according to interior minister Laurent Nunez, who [USN:L1N45T0B2 TEXT:"paused"] the use of stun grenades pending an investigation into the case. Nunez said on Wednesday in a radio interview that about 200 students had been injured, but that it was very rarely the result of police action. “Our primary role is, of course, to protect high school students,” he said. Authorities said that 700 police officers have also been injured, schools have been burned or ransacked, and teachers and members of the public have been attacked. The police have arrested 6,877 people, mostly minors. “France is an anomaly in terms of its use of arms and the number of victims — we have four irreversible injuries in the space of 12 days, and they are minors,” said Sebastian Roche, researcher on policing at the French National Centre for Scientific Research. “It is a level that is unknown in (France’s) contemporary history,” he said. CALLS TO BAN 'LESS LETHAL' WEAPONS Roche said that France stands out in Europe for its use of "less lethal" weapons such as rubber bullets and stun grenades. Such weapons are generally not used for public order policing in Britain, Italy and Germany, aside from Hamburg, and although permitted in Spain, have caused fewer injuries than in France, said Roche. In the Paris suburb of Argenteuil, a 16-year-old student on his way home after finding his school closed was shot by police, injuring his left eye, which may be permanently damaged, his lawyer Sophia Kerbaa told Reuters. It is not clear if he was hit by a rubber bullet or something else, she added. A video viewed by Reuters showed the boy bleeding from his eye. “He was in the wrong place at the wrong time ... he is injured and in shock,” Kerbaa said. The prosecutor investigating the case said that, according to the police account, the injured student “seemed to correspond” to one of two young people who had directed fireworks at police officers, who responded with rubber bullets. The interior ministry did not respond to questions on the case, or that of Eden. Human rights advocates, including Amnesty International, and some politicians have called for “less lethal” weapons to be banned permanently, while police unions say the police need these weapons to enforce order in violent situations and to ensure their own security. “We must withdraw the use of rubber bullets and ... aim for zero injured students. That will allow us to de-escalate,” Mayor Bally Bagayoko of the left-wing France Unbowed party [USN:L6N45T13Z TEXT:"told Reuters"]. Bagayoko joined the protests in his town Saint-Denis, saying he wanted to protect young people from the police. Thierry Clair, a police union representative, said that serious injuries such as Eden’s, or another child losing his hand, were tragedies, but should not call into question France’s policing techniques. He said the problem came instead from the intensity of the violence being committed by some young people who stoked tensions. “How do we respond when people are moving towards confrontation? If we remove intermediate force options, all we are left with is lethal force,” Clair told Reuters. “That is simply inconceivable.”

item.title: Jocelyn Bioh on why Broadway is finally ready for 'School Girls'
item.description: The playwright and actor talks beauty, colorism, and how Broadway has changed in the decade since she wrote the play.
item.dc:creator: Kathryn Lurie
item.content:encoded:
Playwright Jocelyn Bioh during an interview with Reuters in New York City. REUTERS/Brendan McDermid Nearly a decade after Jocelyn Bioh wrote “School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play,” the play itself has barely changed. But the world around it has. The comedy about a group of teenage girls at a Ghanaian boarding school premiered off-Broadway in 2017, launching Bioh’s career as a playwright and going on to become a hit at regional theaters across the United States. But despite its success, Bioh was told it might not belong on Broadway. Now “School Girls” has made it there — following the Broadway success of Bioh’s “Jaja’s African Hair Braiding” in 2023 — and she is finding an audience that responds differently to the play’s exploration of body image, the privileging of lighter skin, known as colorism, and the often brutal social dynamics of girlhood. Beneath its rapid-fire jokes and teenage rivalries is a more painful story about who gets to be considered beautiful — and what people are willing to do to fit that ideal. Speaking in New York City, Bioh discusses what has changed since “School Girls” was first produced, the universality of teenage insecurity and why bringing the play to Broadway feels like coming full circle. This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

How does it feel to finally bring “School Girls” to Broadway? It feels incredibly humbling. This play changed my life. It was the first play of mine that ever got produced. I can very clearly mark what my life was like before opening night of that show and then after. That audiences and critics all still feel the same way nearly a decade later is a reminder that I was on the right track. It also feels doubly exciting because even though it had so much success regionally and has been all over the country, I was told, “It's a great play, but maybe it's not the right fit for a Broadway stage.”

What do you think was meant by that, and what has changed enough for it to be on Broadway now? Broadway shows were very specific then. They didn't have ensembles that looked like the cast of “School Girls.” It was a lot of celebrities, a lot of things that seemed to fit into one specific category or box. The world has shifted. Audiences are different than they were 10 years ago. In a lot of ways, “Jaja's African Hair Braiding” having so much success was a marker that, a Broadway play is just a play that's on Broadway. It doesn't necessarily have to fit a specific category.

Is there anything in the play that hits differently than it did when you first wrote it? The conversation around beauty standards and body image has shifted in the last 10 years. Some would say (for the) better, some would say worse, but we're all aware of it in a different way. The play kicks off with Paulina bullying Nana about her size and her eating. You can feel the audience is immediately on Nana's side. Halfway through the play, she has a moment where she really stands up to Paulina, and every night that moment gets applause. You can feel the audience cheering, almost jumping up ready to fight with her. They're taking off their earrings! We did not have that experience off-Broadway. I think we were in a time where we accepted the idea that if you were somebody who was bigger, you should be losing weight; you should be trying to conform. Our ideas of beauty are very different now. Big ships turn slow, but I appreciate that I can feel that in the audience. Did you rewrite much for this production? Very small things, little jokes that I thought would land better. But the play is still largely the same thing I wrote in 2016. If I were sitting down to write this play now, I don't know that I would be as honest or as vulnerable as I was then, particularly in the moments where Paulina is speaking very directly about how colorism has affected her life. I think I would censor myself a little bit now. I never thought the play would get produced, so I was very free and vulnerable in a way.

Playwright Jocelyn Bioh. REUTERS/Brendan McDermid Why? When you're a playwright and your name starts to grow within the community, you start to have an awareness of the responsibility of your words. And I'm okay with having that responsibility because I know I'm doing something really different. I'm really blowing open how people see Black and African people on a theatrical stage. There's an incredible responsibility to that. The play takes place in Ghana, but these girls feel instantly recognizable. Did you know when you were writing it how universal they would be? I understood that there's a real rich universality we have, particularly in school and friendship dynamics. Those things are evergreen and universal. I knew what I was writing was different, (that) the girls and the people I was reflecting were different, but I didn't want to alienate audiences. That's part of why I added the subtitle. What's something we all know and recognize about the teenage experience? Mean girls. Paulina seems to believe that if she can just become Miss Ghana, she can escape the limits of her life. Is her obsession with beauty really an obsession with power and possibility? Probably. Ultimately, I think she really believes this is going to set her up for a successful life in entertainment. The play is set in 1986, and if you became Miss Ghana, Miss World, Miss Universe — any of those things — you could become a star. This is how we have Vanessa Williams or Halle Berry or Kenya Moore, if you're of the “Real Housewives” persuasion. (Another character,) Eloise, is a former Miss Ghana and did leave. She's come back now living a different life, (signifying that) in order to have success, you've got to get out. In order to have power, you have to get out. Maybe Paulina doesn't see the beauty and power that she can build in her own country. That's reflective of so many immigrant, particularly African immigrant, stories: In order to have success, you need to leave. I don't know if the play were set in 2026, (if) that would be the case now. I think the play would be very different. But for Paulina and her circumstances then, that is what she believed. The play deals so directly with colorism. Do you think colorism is in some ways more sensitive to talk about than racism? They're inextricably linked. The play largely talks about and shows the effects of colorism, but then ends with a global lesson on racism. And we've not moved on from it. When we started rehearsals for the play in August, the biggest news story was Lupita Nyong'o playing Helen of Troy in Christopher Nolan's film (“The Odyssey”). (Her casting) did not fit with whomever's standard of beauty (for) the woman whose face launched a thousand ships. Why didn't it fit? Why were there so many suggestions about, “Well, Zendaya's in the movie, why can't she play that part?” That's a very clear conversation about colorism, whether people are using that word or not.

When I wrote this play, it was really important for me to have that conversation because it had affected my life so much. Revisiting it now, especially in relation to these conversations that are happening globally, I'm like, well, we've not moved on from it. We can't move on from colorism because nobody's moved on from racism. I can't change people's minds. But if people come to see “School Girls” and their implicit bias can shift just a little bit, then I've done my job. The play is extremely funny until you realize how much pain is sitting underneath the humor. How deliberate is that? I really believe that comedy is just a funny way of being serious. Humor and pain are on two different sides of a truth coin. It's all rooted in truth. Paulina is a girl in the world who's trying to be affirmed and validated that she belongs there, that her beauty is widely accepted even if she knows that it's not. The lengths she goes to get there are what's comical, but it's rooted in something real that we all experience. At the end of the day, I'm a comedic writer and I want people to be entertained. But because I know the responsibility of who I'm introducing and the culture I'm introducing, I think there's a responsibility in also educating people. If I can make that medicine go down with a little bit of sugar, honey, agave, whatever you like, I'm willing to go there. The perspectives expressed in Culture Current are the subject’s own and do not necessarily reflect the views of Reuters News.

item.title: Taiwan won't give up freedom, Lai says; Beijing slams 'ulterior motives'
item.description: Taiwan cherishes peace but will not give up its freedom, and there must be respect for the right of Taiwan's people to exist, President Lai Ching-te said on Saturday in a National Day speech, adding that boosting defences is not a provocation.
item.dc:creator: Yimou Lee, Ben Blanchard
item.content:encoded: Taiwan cherishes peace but will not give up its freedom, and there must be respect for the right of Taiwan's people to exist, President Lai Ching-te said on Saturday in a National Day speech, adding that boosting defences is not a provocation. Beijing quickly denounced the speech, saying it "distorts the truth" and reveals "ulterior motives." Democratically governed Taiwan has faced increased military and political pressure from China, which views the island as its own territory over the strong objections of the government in Taipei. Facing China's far larger military, which is adding advanced new weapons such as stealth-fighter jets, aircraft carriers and a huge array of missiles, Taiwan is ramping up [USN:L4N44V0I5 TEXT:"defence spending"] and modernising its armed forces. Peace cannot rely solely on "wishes", Lai said outside the Presidential Office. "Taiwan cherishes peace, but we will not give up our freedom. We are open to exchanges, but will not accept subordination." Taiwan's resolve is not only a matter of its survival in the face of "authoritarian expansion", he added. "It is about whether the international community still believes that force cannot override rules, and that the powerful cannot strip a people of their right to determine their own future." DEFENCE INVESTMENT NOT 'PROVOCATION' China's Taiwan Affairs Office said Lai's speech "disregards facts, distorts the truth, misleads the public, and reveals ulterior motives", accusing him of stubbornly clinging to "Taiwan independence" separatist thinking and exaggerating the "threat from the mainland". "There is only one China in the world, and Taiwan is part of China – this is the true status quo in the Taiwan Strait," the office said. Taiwan's future "can and must be decided jointly by all the Chinese people, including our compatriots in Taiwan," China's state television CCTV reported the office's spokesperson as saying. China, which has never renounced the use of force to bring Taiwan under its control, calls the president a "separatist" and has rebuffed his offers of talks.
