The US welcomes Lai's commitment to maintaining peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait, a senior US administration official said, adding, in reference to China, that "a routine speech is no justification for aggressive or coercive actions". The United States is Taiwan's most important international backer despite the lack of formal diplomatic ties. Lai did not use his usual wording that neither side of the Taiwan Strait is "subordinate" to the other, but did use a phrase from Jesus' Sermon on the Mount, saying Taiwan must become a "'city upon a hill,' built with courage and confidence". Lai said his government's increased investment in defence aimed to deter war, not provoke it. "And we are strengthening our self-defence not to abandon dialogue, but to ensure that dialogue can take place on the basis of parity and dignity," he told the crowd at the event, where he also watched military displays and dancing performances. "There must be respect for the right of the people of Taiwan to exist." US YET TO APPROVE NEW ARMS PACKAGE In 2024, shortly after Lai's first National Day speech as president, China held war games around the island but did not do so last year. Its last [USN:L1N3Y000J TEXT:"war games"] near Taiwan were in late December, following news of an $11-billion US arms deal for Taipei, the largest ever. US President Donald Trump has yet to approve a second package, worth [USN:L1N45T00J TEXT:"$14 billion."] Lai said he welcomed the United States and China managing their competition through [USN:L6N45K195 TEXT:"dialogue"] and reducing the risk of conflict and war, in what a Taiwanese official told reporters was a direct response to last month's [USN:L1N45H0FW TEXT:"China-US summit"] in Washington. But Lai urged democracies in the Indo-Pacific region to join forces to retain the status quo of peace and stability in the region. Taiwan's National Day is held on the anniversary of a 1911 uprising that led to the overthrow of China's last imperial dynasty and the establishment of the Republic of China. The Republican government fled to Taiwan in 1949 after losing a civil war with Mao Zedong's communists, and the Republic of China remains the island's formal name.

item.title: Cam Talbot, Kent Johnson power Jackets' shootout win over Penguins
item.description: Kent Johnson scored in the first round of the shootout and Cam Talbot made it stand up in his season debut, fueling the host Columbus Blue Jackets to a 3-2 victory over the Pittsburgh Penguins on Friday.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Kent Johnson scored in the first round of the shootout and Cam Talbot made it stand up in his season debut, fueling the host Columbus Blue Jackets to a 3-2 victory over the Pittsburgh Penguins on Friday. All four games between the teams last season ventured past regulation before Friday's game followed suit. Johnson scored by sending the puck between the pads of Sergei Murashov in the first round. Talbot denied Rickard Rakell and Ben Kindel in the first and third rounds, respectively, while former Blue Jacket Egor Chinakhov's attempt sailed wide of the net. Columbus defenseman Damon Severson collected a goal and an assist in his season debut. He was activated from the injured/non-roster list after undergoing shoulder surgery in April. Mathieu Olivier also scored and Cole Sillinger notched two assists for the Blue Jackets, who dictated play by enjoying a decisive advantage in both shots (45-22) and faceoff wins (30-15). Talbot, who made 20 saves, was suiting up for his ninth NHL team after signing a one-year contract with Columbus on Sept. 14. The well-rested Blue Jackets were playing in their first game since recording a 4-1 loss to the Utah Mammoth on Saturday. Pittsburgh's Bryan Rust scored for the second time in as many games and Evgeni Malkin also tallied. Murashov turned aside 43 shots for the Penguins, who have lost three in a row (0-2-1). Despite being outshot 33-10 over the first two periods, Pittsburgh forged a 2-2 tie at 3:19 of the third. Malkin did the honors after backhanding home a loose puck following defenseman Erik Karlsson's shot from the point. Defenseman Zach Werenski secured the attention of Pittsburgh's Rust and Rakell before wiring a cross-zone feed from the top of the right circle to Severson. He converted from the lower left circle to open the scoring at 10:52 of the first period. Olivier doubled the advantage at 11:40 of the second period after his shot from the right circle caromed off both the post and the skate of Murashov before entering the net. The goal was the second of the season for Olivier. Rust responded less than three minutes later by skating wide of Severson before tucking the puck past Talbot. --Field Level Media

item.title: Isaias kills two, leaves thousands without power after landfall
item.description: The National Hurricane Center expects storm surges, flash flooding, damaging winds and a risk of tornadoes across parts of the US Southeast.
item.dc:creator: Rhea Abraham, Rajveer Pardesi, Marianna Parraga
item.content:encoded: Two people died and about 800,000 Florida, Alabama and Georgia residents were without power after Hurricane Isaias made landfall early on Saturday, weakening to a post-tropical cyclone, according to local authorities and electricity monitoring services. Authorities in Florida had received no search and rescue requests shortly after landfall in a sign of limited impact, Governor Ron DeSantis said. But hazardous conditions remained and storm surges, flash flooding, damaging winds and a risk of tornadoes across parts of the US Southeast were expected, the National Hurricane Center said. The tornado threat is expected to continue on Saturday across parts of the Florida Panhandle, Georgia and the Carolinas, the NHC said. In Florida, power restoration was marked as priority, authorities said, while highways, bridges and airports were reopening, and teams were assessing the damage. "They're going to make assessments this morning, and I think that'll give us a good sense about the future for the rapidity of the power restoration," DeSantis told a press conference in Tallahassee. Some 16,000 utility linemen had prepared to respond to the storm, he said. More than 430,000 customers in Florida, over 280,000 in Alabama and some 100,000 in Georgia lost power as the storm hit shore, according to tracking firm PowerOutage.us. In Alabama and Florida, two people were killed by falling trees, according to local media and authorities. Alabama's emergency management agency said the downed trees and power lines made travel hazardous in Houston County, which is under a flash flood warning. "Due to the impacts of Hurricane Isaias, all Houston County roads are closed until further notice," it posted on X. Isaias rapidly lost wind speed after hitting the Florida coast as a Category 2 hurricane, the first of the 2026 Atlantic season. It is expected to produce gusty winds well inland before weakening below gale force later on Saturday, the NHC said. On Saturday, oil and gas producer Shell (SHEL.L) said it was beginning to redeploy personnel to its Mars, Olympus, Ursa, Vito, and Appomattox assets in the Gulf. President Donald Trump, asked about hurricane preparations on Friday, told reporters outside the White House that it was "under control." Emergency declarations were approved in Florida and Alabama to ensure federal resources would be available to respond to Isaias, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on X. "There's also a lot of hazards post-storm that people should be careful of, but so far, we've had a lot of assets in place that have not been called on," DeSantis told FOX News early on Saturday.

item.title: Trump says Norway has 'indelible stain' for not awarding him Nobel Peace Prize
item.description: Each year of his presidency, Trump has expressed disappointment at his failure to win.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Bogage
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump reiterated his complaints on Friday about not receiving the Nobel Peace Prize, calling it a disgraceful and embarrassing decision that had left a stain on Norway, which hosts the Nobel committee. Trump unleashed on Norway hours after the committee awarded this year's prize to [USN:L8N45V0JG TEXT:"Navi Pillay,"] a former International Criminal Court judge who oversaw a UN report that concluded Israel committed genocide in Gaza. Trump called Pillay a "mystery person" during a campaign rally in Syracuse, New York. "I never heard of the person. Nobody did." Each year of his presidency, Trump has expressed disappointment at his failure to win the prize. "This is an indelible stain on the country of Norway and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision," Trump said. He listed a number of conflicts that he [USN:L1N3UC0RP TEXT:"claimed a role in resolving"] and said he has helped prevent wars from breaking out between North and South Korea, Japan and North Korea, and China and Taiwan, without providing evidence. "The Nobel Peace Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really enemies of civilization. And we will not forget, Norway," he said.

item.title: India detains thousands, locks down Delhi to foil election chief protest
item.description: Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel deployed across the city, mobile internet services were suspended and dozens of metro stations and markets were shut as authorities moved to stop a rally organized by the Cockroach movement.
item.dc:creator: Saurabh Sharma, Sarita Singh, Sakshi Dayal
item.content:encoded: Police detained more than 2,000 protesters and the founder of the "Cockroach" youth movement in Delhi on Saturday as security forces [USN:L1N45V075 TEXT:"locked down"] parts of the capital to thwart a rally demanding the resignation of India's election chief. Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed across the city, mobile internet services were suspended in the central business district and dozens of metro stations and markets were shut as authorities moved to stop a demonstration organised by the Cockroach movement. The protest was aimed at Chief Election Commissioner [USN:L4N45K0DB TEXT:"Gyanesh Kumar"] over a [USN:L1N45V037 TEXT:"revision of voter lists"] that critics say disproportionately benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The movement had planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar in central Delhi, but the area was sealed off by security forces before the demonstration began. A home ministry official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Reuters more than 2,000 people were detained in Delhi. Local media said about 400 protesters were held in India's financial hub, Mumbai. There was no immediate comment from police on the detentions. Small protests broke out elsewhere in Delhi, including at a popular crafts market and the memorial to freedom movement leader Mahatma Gandhi, with demonstrators demanding Kumar's resignation. "Long live the revolution," some young protesters chanted as police chased them and dragged scores of others into buses to be taken away, even as more arrived, a Reuters witness said. "This is violating the rights of the people and the country will not tolerate this anymore," Yogendra Solanki told Reuters as police escorted him away. MOVEMENT LEADERS HELD Police detained Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke and senior leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka when their flight from Mumbai landed in Delhi, the group said in a statement. Television footage showed Dipke challenging officers who approached him on board the aircraft. "I have come to be arrested, arrest me ... I am not afraid of you guys," he said. "No, this is not an arrest," one officer replied. "Please cooperate." The movement condemned what it called the "authoritarian detention" of its leaders, demanded their release and vowed to continue protesting. "We will continue our protest tomorrow, day after ... until Gyanesh Kumar resigns. We will be on the streets," CJP leader Ajinkya Shinde told reporters. CJP also said authorities refused to provide updates on the leaders' whereabouts or health, even after news arrived of the death of Dipke's grandmother. Police said Dipke was informed of her death and was offered help to return home for the funeral. Some opposition lawmakers and former chief ministers Mamata Banerjee of West Bengal, Arvind Kejriwal of Delhi, and Pinarayi Vijayan of Kerala were also detained, TV channels showed. Representatives of two digital news outlets said police briefly detained four of their reporters while they were covering the demonstrations. A Reuters journalist was also detained briefly before being released. Across the capital of about 20 million people, security forces set up checkpoints on major roads and entry points, boarded buses searching for protesters and inspected vehicles. Barricades and concrete blocks disrupted traffic while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear-gas launchers guarded key routes. NEW CHALLENGE TO MODI The demonstrations represent one of the most serious tests yet for Modi, stemming from allegations that election authorities improperly revised voter rolls ahead of recent state polls. Protests intensified after the Indian Express reported last week that two election commissioners had questioned Kumar's voter-list revisions that removed roughly 130 million names from voter lists. Kumar has not commented but the Election Commission and the BJP have denied allegations of wrongdoing. The BJP says its electoral success reflects Modi's popularity and India's economic growth, and accuses opposition parties of spreading misinformation. The near [USN:L6N45U0IF TEXT:"daily protests"] come just months after demonstrations over exam paper leaks forced his [USN:L1N43R02E TEXT:"education minister to quit"]. The unrest also comes ahead of a series of important state elections beginning in early 2027. Rahul Gandhi, leader of the main opposition Congress party, said Modi's opponents would not back down. A senior BJP member, Ravi Shankar Prasad, said the party was not opposed to demonstrations but the street protests had been "weaponised" by rivals due to election defeats. DELETIONS AFFECTED STATE POLLS, OPPOSITION ALLEGES Opposition parties say the deletions affected the outcome of recent state elections won by the BJP and have cast a shadow over voting in the world's largest democracy. Election Commission data show about 130 million voter entries were removed during the verification exercise, including 63 million people who had relocated, 30 million who could not be traced and 28 million who had died. The commission says the removals relate to entries identified during the draft revision process and that any eligible voter incorrectly deleted can re-enrol.

item.title: Super Micro contractor pleads guilty in scheme to divert AI servers with Nvidia chips to China
item.description: Ting-Wei "Willy" Sun pleaded guilty to four counts.
item.dc:creator: Karen Freifeld, Jaspreet Singh
item.content:encoded: A contractor linked to Super Micro Computer (SMCI.O) has pleaded guilty in a scheme to illegally export computer servers containing advanced Nvidia (NVDA.O) AI chips to China, a federal court filing showed on Friday. Ting-Wei "Willy" Sun pleaded guilty to four counts, including conspiracies to violate US export controls, smuggle goods from the US, defraud the country and obstruct justice. He entered the plea on Thursday in U.S. District Court in Manhattan. The United States and China are competing for dominance in AI, with both investing billions of dollars in a technology seen as critical to economic growth, national security and military capabilities. In March, [USN:L1N4071M5 TEXT:"prosecutors charged"] Sun and two others associated with Super Micro, including a co-founder of the AI-server maker, with conspiring to divert about $2.5 billion worth of US AI technology to China in violation of export laws. The scheme began around October 2023, with Sun and others conspiring to export servers from a US manufacturer, widely believed to be Super Micro, to China without the required licenses, according to the indictment. Asked for comment on the guilty plea, California-based Super Micro referred to its prior statements that the company was not named as a defendant in the indictment and that it had no impact on its business operations. [USN:L4N40Q1GS TEXT:"Super Micro"] terminated Sun and cut ties with the other defendants earlier this year. A lawyer for Sun declined to comment. Also indicted were the co-founder Yih-Shyan "Wally" Liaw and Ruei-Tsang "Steven" Chang, who was a sales manager at Super Micro's Taiwan office, while Sun was a contractor. A lawyer for Liaw - who co-founded Super Micro in 1993 and joined its board in 2023 - did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Chang's lawyer could not immediately be reached for comment. The indictment described Sun as a broker and “fixer” who facilitated orders and took steps to conceal the scheme. He helped stage "dummy" servers in December 2025 and made false statements to a US Department of Commerce officer during an inspection of supposedly stored servers, which had already been diverted to China, according to the indictment. Washington has restricted sales of advanced AI chips to China, citing national security concerns. The indictment said Nvidia's B200, H100 and H200 graphics processing units, and servers containing them, were subject to the restrictions.

item.title: US lifts sanctions on daughter of Myanmar military-linked businessman
item.description: The United States lifted on Friday sanctions on the daughter of a Myanmar businessman accused of supporting the country's military, according to the US Treasury Department's website, after she filed a suit seeking removal from the blacklist.
item.dc:creator: Simon Lewis
item.content:encoded: The United States lifted on Friday sanctions on the daughter of a Myanmar businessman accused of supporting the country's military, according to the US Treasury Department's website, after she filed a suit seeking removal from the blacklist. The move comes after Reuters reported this week that the Trump administration had [USN:L6N45T16N TEXT:"opened talks with Myanmar's military-installed government"], reversing US policy that sought to isolate the generals who overthrew elected leaders in 2021. A State Department spokesperson said the decision to remove Myanmar national Theint Win Htet from the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List (SDN List) "reflects the administration’s determination that this designation no longer effectively supports US policy objectives related to Burma." "The administration is using a range of tools to advance key priorities regarding Burma, such as combating scam centers, improving Burma's domestic operating environment for US businesses, and encouraging a peace process to address the ongoing violence and humanitarian crisis," the spokesperson said, using the country's previous name. After the 2021 coup, former President Joe Biden's administration imposed sanctions on senior Myanmar military officers and companies it accused of providing support for the military junta, which triggered a nationwide civil war that has killed an estimated 100,000 people and displaced more than 3.5 million. The Treasury in January 2024 [USN:S0N3D107F TEXT:"targeted the "][USN:S0N3D107F TEXT:"Shwe Byain Phyu Group of Companies"], its founder Thein Win Zaw and his family, saying the company imported and distributed petroleum on behalf of the military and that the family owned at least 20 companies closely associated with the regime. Thein Win Zaw's adult daughter, Theint Win Htet, sued the Biden administration seeking her removal from the SDN List, but her case was dismissed in February 2025. The sanctions freeze any US assets of those targeted and generally bar Americans from dealing with them. The US in July 2025 [USN:L1N3TM01T TEXT:"lifted sanctions"] on several other Myanmar nationals and a firm under sanctions for aiding the military. Theint Win Htet filed a new complaint in July this year, arguing that she has no active role in her father's business affairs, adding that the sanctions had interrupted her studies in the US, where she completed a bachelor's degree at New York University and was enrolled in a master's program at Columbia University. "Plaintiff’s US credit cards have been blocked, her foreign bank accounts have been restricted, closed, or refused, and she has been unable to complete her university studies in the United States," said the complaint by Theint Win Htet, who said in the complaint she now lives with her mother in Bangkok. Her mother was removed from the sanctions list last year. Campaign group Justice For Myanmar denounced the US move at a time when it said the Myanmar military was escalating attacks on civilians. "It is deplorable that the US government continues to delist Myanmar cronies and their family members that provide funding for the junta's terror," the group said. Theint Win Htet's lawyer, Washington-based sanctions specialist Erich Ferrari, filed a notice with the US District Court for the District of Columbia on Friday voluntarily dismissing the lawsuit after her delisting. Ferrari declined to comment.

item.title: Erik Prince's forces suffer battlefield loss in Congo, former UFC fighter among wounded, sources say
item.description: Popular former UFC fighter Tim Kennedy was among the wounded in an ambush that killed or wounded at least 20 people deployed by Vectus Global.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Donati
item.content:encoded: Blackwater founder Erik Prince's forces suffered a major battlefield loss in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo in mid-September when enemy forces ambushed them, killing and wounding at least 20 people, including a popular former UFC fighter, sources close to the government and his company said. The frontline clash shows how Prince, an ally and supporter of US President Donald Trump, has taken on an expanded role in Congo through his company Vectus Global. The company, which also operates in Haiti and other parts of Africa, provides consulting and security services and previously [USN:L6N3XA0X0 TEXT:"helped Congo’s army"] secure the city of Uvira in South Kivu against Rwanda-backed rebels who control swathes of the east. A veteran special operator reported on his podcast earlier this week that former US Green Beret and Ultimate Fighting Championship contestant Tim Kennedy was injured in Congo. The involvement of Prince's forces and the number of casualties have not previously been reported. The attack in South Kivu on September 17 left about 20 dead and wounded, two sources working with Congo's government said. The dead included at least seven Congolese and a former member of New Zealand's Special Forces, while the wounded included Kennedy and another foreign contractor, the sources said. A Vectus Global representative declined to comment. The company has not previously suffered casualties in Congo, a source with direct knowledge of the operation said. One of the sources who works for Congo's government said that Rwandan forces backing the M23 rebels may have surprised them by tracking a drone used for surveillance operations to their location. Spokespeople for the Congolese and Rwandan governments and for the M23 did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Kennedy, the former mixed martial arts fighter, survived the attack with three gunshot wounds to the leg, three sources said, and is being treated at the Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in the suburbs of Washington. Kennedy has a popular podcast channel and millions of followers on social media. Trump is a fan of UFC, [USN:L6N42N00Z TEXT:"hosting fights"] at the White House this year. The US State Department and Walter Reed declined to comment. Kennedy's parents did not respond to requests for comment. A Congolese security source, who said some 20 people were wounded and killed in the attack, added that villagers were likely among the casualties as well. Reuters spoke to at least 10 sources either with direct knowledge of the attack or briefed on the outcome. PRINCE TOOK EXPANDED ROLE IN CONGO'S CONFLICT Prince's initial mandate in Congo was to secure and improve revenue collection from the country's vast mineral reserves, which have been plundered for decades, fuelling relentless conflict in the east. But in January and early February, his forces deployed to Uvira after Washington helped broker a deal for Rwandan-backed rebels to withdraw from the strategic town. The size of Prince's forces in Congo is unclear. One of the sources with direct knowledge of the attack said the Vectus team was travelling between locations when the ambush took place and its sophistication suggested Rwandan forces were involved. "It reinforces the need for DRC sovereignty to be restored. It's an incredibly dangerous place right now," the source said. Two other sources said the ambush was carried out by the Rwandan military. Prince is the founder of now-defunct private military firm Blackwater, some of whose members were pardoned in 2020 for killing Iraqi civilians. The State Department has said it does not have any contracts with Prince in Congo, though US officials have said they plan to work [USN:L1N43O0RW TEXT:"more closely with Vectus Global"] in Haiti. The deal for Rwandan-backed rebels to withdraw from Uvira was part of [USN:L6N3XA0X0 TEXT:"wider agreements"] brokered by the Trump administration to try to end the conflict in eastern Congo. POPULAR PODCASTER Kennedy, a father of four, has posted his views on politics, culture, fitness and more on social media. He also runs a popular YouTube podcast in which he interviews UFC fighters, veterans, cultural disruptors and others. He has often posted about his family, including four young children. In late August, he posted about having "incredible conversations about what being a man means and what sacrifice really looks like" with his son. He did not disclose details about his upcoming trip to Congo. The United Nations and Western powers say Rwanda backs M23, even exercising command and control over the group. Rwanda denies this. Fighting in the decades-long conflict flared early last year, with M23 fighters making rapid gains in the east, which is rich in tantalum, gold, lithium and other minerals.

item.title: Anthropic discloses fake tip to police among new rogue AI incidents
item.description: It is the first known instance in which AI appears to have tried to communicate a bogus tip to authorities, despite instructions not to create accounts or submit anything destructive, while not explicitly barred from submitting forms.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: An Anthropic artificial intelligence model submitted a false homicide tip to a Philadelphia police website, among a string of incidents the AI company disclosed on Friday detailing Claude models' unsanctioned manipulation of some government websites. It is the first known instance in which a rogue AI appears to have tried to communicate a bogus tip to authorities, despite instructions not to create accounts or submit anything destructive, while not explicitly barred from submitting forms. The cases are the latest examples of rogue or undesired behavior by the AI models of tech companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI. They add fuel to national concerns about the fast-advancing technology amid reports of corporate network hacks by AI agents, and researchers' warnings of an eventual existential threat to humanity. Many of the cases Anthropic revealed involved websites run by federal, state and local agencies. Anthropic said it briefed the White House and notified all the agencies involved, but did not disclose who those parties were. "Super intelligence companies must immediately disclose incidents involving their models and follow with swift, decisive action to remedy any and all harm," FTC Director of Public Affairs Joe Gabriel Simonson said on X. This process was "not optional," he said, adding that the Super Intelligence Force would fulfill its responsibility. The FTC said Anthropic disclosed to the SI Force on Friday its late September discovery of incidents involving what the task force called "unauthorized and fraudulent use of government and other systems". TIP ATTRIBUTED TO AUTOMATED TEST PROCESS On Friday, Philadelphia police said Anthropic notified them of the spurious tip this week, and attributed the submissions to an automated testing process. "The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the city is unacceptable," they said. The July 18 tip purported to come from someone who might have information about the case, police added. "I may have information regarding this case," Anthropic's model wrote in its submission. "I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around (the street named on the page) during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant." The brackets featured in Anthropic's statement. Previous incidents have involved AI agents hacking into vulnerable systems or commandeering unsanctioned platforms to communicate with one another. In September, Anthropic rival OpenAI apologized for the hacking of an Australian health data portal by a rogue AI agent, the first known instance of an AI agent exploiting a government website. A BOGUS TIP In two cases described on Friday, Anthropic’s models obtained for free public data normally only available for a fee. Another instanced revealed an obscure flaw that allowed use of a public tool hosted by a university. Claude models were also able to bypass restrictions by using free services that shorten URLs. Philadelphia police said the tip "was flagged as spam and was never forwarded to the Real-Time Crime Center for investigative vetting or dissemination." Knowingly giving false reports to law enforcement authorities is a misdemeanor under Pennsylvania law, which specifies "a person", however. This includes "information relating to an offense or incident when he knows he has no information relating to such offense or incident." Police quoted Anthropic as telling them the test process was stopped after discovery of the incident. The false tip was submitted through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com concerning an unsolved homicide. Police said they had no evidence of unauthorized access to their systems or compromise of their data.

item.title: Moroccan king says migration cooperation model with Spain hit limit
item.description: King Mohammed VI said on Friday that Morocco's efforts to curb irregular migration had produced "concrete results," but that the current cooperation model with Spain had reached its limits amid recurring crises.
item.dc:creator: Ahmed Eljechtimi
item.content:encoded: King Mohammed VI said on Friday that Morocco's efforts to curb irregular migration had produced "concrete results," but that the current cooperation model with Spain had reached its limits amid recurring crises. At least 70,000 people [USN:S8N3VJ0CQ TEXT:"crossed"] from Morocco into the enclave of Ceuta in July. Most have returned but thousands, including minors, [USN:L8N45Q015 TEXT:"remained"]. Speaking at the parliament's opening, the king cited "obsolete" and "unrealistic" Spanish court decisions that hindered cooperation on migration. "They are regrettably impeding the repatriation of minors and of fake asylum seekers, while fueling the greed of criminal networks," he said. Since the Ceuta migration crisis, [USN:L1N45A0G3 TEXT:"Spanish opposition"] parties have blamed Pedro Sanchez's government and [USN:L1N4520W0 TEXT:"accused"] Rabat of facilitating the crossing. Morocco rejected the accusations, blaming the crossing on social media and misinterpretations of a court ruling that appeared to open a legal loophole for arrivals by sea. Morocco's partnership with Spain was a "sovereign choice" and "it will never be subject to any pressure, threat, or blackmail," the king said. He added that Morocco would propose a vision centred on shared development, economic competitiveness and regional stability to its partners. Relations between Morocco and Spain have improved since Spain backed Morocco's autonomy plan for Western Sahara in 2022. But bilateral ties have faced a [USN:L1N45N08Q TEXT:"test"] since the Ceuta migration crisis. The king [USN:S8N3SV012 TEXT:"appointed"] Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri as the country's first female prime minister, after her party finished on top in the September 23 election. He urged members of parliament to put young people at the heart of public policies.

item.title: Strong Panama quake shakes nation, but avoids major destruction
item.description: A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck southern Panama on Friday, damaging buildings and sending thousands into the streets, but the country appeared to escape widespread destruction or deaths.
item.dc:creator: Elida Moreno, Dave Sherwood
item.content:encoded: A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck southern Panama on Friday, damaging buildings and sending thousands into the streets, but the country appeared to escape widespread destruction or deaths. The US Geological Survey said the earthquake hit at a depth of 12.6 km (7.8 miles), with an epicenter in a sparsely populated area about 200 km (124 miles) from the capital, and that some casualties were possible. In the following hours, even as more than 40 aftershocks rattled the isthmus nation, the Panama Canal and Cobre Panama copper mine reported normal operations and the Tocumen International Airport lifted a suspension on flights. Office workers in the upscale business hub of downtown Panama City fretted about how to get home in the snarl of traffic, after the quake sent thousands into the streets. Juan Sanchez, a 37-year-old economy ministry employee, waited for a bus he said he doubted would arrive. "They evacuated all of these buildings. Everyone is outside. Now the problem is, how do we get home?" President Raul Mulino traveled to Penonome, a city about halfway between the epicenter and Panama City, where some buildings collapsed and a church was damaged. Despite the force of Friday's tremor, the country appeared to have been spared the [USN:L6N44903E TEXT:"destruction"] of other recent powerful quakes in the [USN:L6N42X19G TEXT:"region"], with no deaths or injuries immediately reported. Back-to-back quakes in Venezuela in June killed several thousand people, while a quake in Colombia in August killed more than 300. An exposure report by the USGS estimated about 43,000 Panamanians lived in areas with at least severe exposure to the quake. This compares to nearly 1.4 million in the area of the twin quakes in Venezuela and over 1.6 million in the quake-hit zone of western Colombia. PROLONGED VIBRATIONS Nestor Luque, director of Panama's geosciences institute, attributed the quake to the Azuero Sona Fault System that he said contained a massive buildup of pressure that is occasionally released. "The seismic signals have traveled throughout the national territory and that is why it could be felt everywhere." In Panama City, Luque said he counted 40 seconds of vibrations, though other areas may have felt even longer tremors. Sabina Rios, who was on the sixth floor of an old US military-era building in Panama City, said the shaking was unusually strong and prolonged. "The quake felt strong and lasted a long time, the longest I’ve felt in years,” Rios said. Victor Pinzon, a 48-year-old maintenance worker, told Reuters he had watched high-rise window cleaners ride out the shaking. “It’s a miracle they didn’t get killed,” he said. “They looked like they were swinging in a hammock.” Strong earthquakes are not common in Panama, and some elderly residents were in tears as they evacuated into the streets. “We’re scared. It’s just the two of us old folks here. The house has cracked, and we’re afraid it could fall on us,” said Ricardo Brown, 74, in Herrera province in southern Panama, where he said he saw a number of damaged homes. Omar Smith, who heads Panama's civil protection agency, told news outlet Telemetro Reporta that impacts had also been reported in Chitre, the capital of Herrera, and along the coast in Los Santos province. The USGS estimated economic losses could amount to 1% to 10% of Panama's gross domestic product, and electricity provider Naturgy reported power outages in six provinces. Panama was due to hold a national evacuation drill on Monday of next week to test the country's emergency response.

item.title: Is it legal for the US to livestream the Fort Hood shooter's execution?
item.description: Here's what US law says about public executions and death by firing squad.
item.dc:creator: Jan Wolfe
item.content:encoded: The Pentagon [USN:L1N45U11T TEXT:"said"] on Thursday that it would livestream the firing squad execution of the man who killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, raising questions about the legality of the unprecedented announcement. Here's what US law says about public executions and death by firing squad. IS DEATH BY FIRING SQUAD LEGAL IN THE US? Yes. The US Supreme Court said in a unanimous 1879 decision that execution by firing squad is not "cruel and unusual punishment" prohibited by the Constitution. The justices last year cleared the way for South Carolina to carry out its first execution by firing squad in decades. Five states currently allow executions by firing squad: Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina, and Utah. The Trump administration earlier this year said it would allow execution by firing squad in the federal prison system. The US Army also once regularly carried out executions by firing squad of US soldiers found guilty of desertion or other offenses. Hundreds of US soldiers were sentenced to death during the Civil War from 1861 to 1865. Under the Uniform Code of Military Justice, the president is the only person who can approve a death sentence for a member of the US armed services. President Donald Trump on October 5 signed off on the Pentagon's plan to execute the Fort Hood gunman, Nidal Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist. CAN EXECUTIONS BE BROADCAST? Executions in the US were once public spectacles, but in the last century have been carried out in correctional facilities away from the public eye. In 1936, a man convicted of rape was hanged in front of thousands in Owensboro, Kentucky, while the following year, hundreds watched a public hanging in Missouri. A US law prohibits the recording or broadcasting of executions in the federal prison system. But military regulations have not applied that same prohibition to military executions. Hasan was convicted of premeditated murder by a military jury in 2013, following a court-martial trial. State laws regulate who can witness executions, generally limiting access to authorized officials, family members, legal counsel, and a handful of media representatives. Courts have long rejected lawsuits brought by media organizations seeking broader public access to executions. In 2001, a judge denied a request by an internet company to livestream the lethal injection execution of Timothy McVeigh, an anti-government militant who bombed a federal building in Oklahoma City in 1995, killing 168 people. The Justice Department did provide a restricted, closed-circuit television broadcast exclusively for survivors of the bombing and victims' families. COULD HASAN CHALLENGE HIS EXECUTION IN COURT? While Hasan has exhausted his direct appeals within the military justice system, he can still challenge his underlying conviction and sentence in the federal civilian court system. Such a challenge, known as a federal habeas corpus proceeding, provides another layer of review before a death sentence is carried out. Even if unsuccessful, that move could stall the execution, potentially for years. Hasan's execution is currently set for December 3. Hasan could also file a civil rights lawsuit seeking to challenge the method of his execution, legal experts said. Hasan told a panel of military mental health experts in 2010 that he wished he had been killed during the attack because it would have meant God had chosen him for martyrdom, an indication that he may not exercise all his legal options. Hasan acted as his own attorney during his 2013 military trial and offered almost no defense. WHAT ABOUT INTERNATIONAL LAW? The United Nations has condemned the plan to livestream Hasan's execution, saying it is a cruel and inhumane form of punishment that violates an international human rights treaty adopted in 1984 known as the Convention Against Torture. But that treaty, like many other international legal frameworks, is not judicially enforceable within the US court system. "The livestreaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture," said the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights.

item.title: How the US plan to livestream an execution compares with global practice
item.description: Governments have spent years trying to limit the circulation of violent execution footage.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The U.S. military plans to livestream the Dec. 3 execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 Fort Hood shooting. If carried out as planned, death penalty experts said it would mark the first known broadcast or livestream of a lawful execution. Executions are generally conducted behind prison walls, and internet platforms and governments have spent years trying to limit the circulation of violent execution footage. HAS A LAWFUL EXECUTION EVER BEEN LIVESTREAMED OR BROADCAST TO THE PUBLIC BEFORE? Death penalty experts consulted by Reuters said they were unaware of any previous lawful execution that had been livestreamed or broadcast to a public audience. Execution footage has occasionally emerged after the event. The hanging of former Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein in 2006, for example, was seen around the world after official and unofficial recordings circulated online and through broadcasters, though it was not shown live. Broadcasts and livestreams today are common for court proceedings, parliamentary debates and other state functions, but not for judicial executions. HOW UNUSUAL IS THIS COMPARED WITH MODERN EXECUTION PRACTICES AROUND THE WORLD? Public executions have become rare worldwide, with most countries that retain the death penalty carrying out executions away from public view. According to Amnesty International, public executions recorded in recent years have largely been concentrated in Iran and Taliban-run Afghanistan. The execution would also be notable in the United States. Public executions largely disappeared during the 20th century, and death penalty experts cited by Reuters said the last legally sanctioned public execution took place in 1936. Hasan's execution would be the first carried out by firing squad by the U.S. military since the 1945 execution of Eddie Slovik, who was convicted of desertion during World War Two. HOW HAS THE INTERNET CHANGED THE CIRCULATION OF EXECUTION FOOTAGE? The internet has transformed execution imagery from a local event into content capable of reaching global audiences within minutes. Militant groups such as Islamic State became notorious for producing professionally edited execution videos that were distributed online as propaganda and recruitment tools. Criminal organisations, including Mexican drug cartels, have also circulated violent footage to intimidate rivals and project power. The ability of users to rapidly copy, repost and redistribute content has made it more difficult for governments and technology companies to control the spread of such material. WHAT HAS BEEN THE REACTION FROM GOVERNMENTS AND TECH COMPANIES? Governments and technology companies have generally moved in the opposite direction, attempting to reduce rather than expand access to graphic execution footage. Major social media platforms have spent years removing execution videos linked to extremist organisations and other violent groups. One of the first public governmental reactions came from New Zealand, whose chief censor said authorities would have little practical ability to prevent residents from accessing a livestream while it was taking place. Livestreams pose particular challenges for platforms because footage can be viewed, copied and redistributed before moderation systems can intervene. Even countries that still conduct public executions have often restricted filming and broadcast rights. Saudi Arabia historically carried out public executions before spectators, but recording them was prohibited and such public executions had largely ceased by 2019. (This story has been corrected to fix the year to 2001, not 2021, in paragraph 15.)

item.title: US imposes sanctions on ICC hours after former judge wins Nobel Peace Prize
item.description: Navi Pillay sat in the court's appeals chamber.
item.dc:creator: Humeyra Pamuk, Steve Holland, Anthony Deutsch
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump's administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court on Friday, hours after one of its [USN:L8N45V0JG TEXT:"former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize"], putting Washington on a diplomatic collision course with European allies. The court denounced the move as an "assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order," and called on its 125 member states to take action to defend it. "The Court cannot stand alone. Its fate now rests also in the hands of the states that created it," it said in a statement. "This is not just about defending a single institution, but about safeguarding the international order grounded upon the rule of law. History will judge this moment." The Trump administration has long been hostile to the court, founded in 2002 [USN:L6N3VQ0DE TEXT:"to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide"], and has previously [USN:O8N42O02H TEXT:"imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges"]. Friday's move goes much further, potentially punishing companies that provide services to the court itself, amounting to an unprecedented attack on an institution founded on an international treaty. The US initially signed the Rome Statute that founded the court but never ratified it. "President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement, first published by Reuters. "That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate." SANCTIONS INCLUDE GRACE PERIOD The US Treasury announced the sanctions with a six-month initial grace period, and some other exemptions that would allow some transactions for telecoms, software, payment of pensions and transactions related to detainees. Rubio said the sanctions had been structured to give the court and its member states an opportunity to address US concerns, and would be adjusted if those demands were not met. Washington has denounced the ICC over arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and an investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan, which the ICC says is "deprioritized." Rubio in his statement cited calls from outside experts for the ICC to prosecute American service members, border patrol agents and elected leaders. ICC officials have not taken steps toward such prosecutions. "The sanctions are intended to undermine the rule of law internationally and the work that an independent judicial institution is doing," ICC Deputy Prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan told Reuters. "Our work will continue across all our situations, our investigations and our prosecutions." EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on social media that the six-month period "offers a window for dialogue" but added that the bloc "has options to ensure that (the ICC) can continue its vital work." Belgium's foreign minister called for an EU blocking statute to be activated to protect the court. The ICC has issued arrest warrants against more than 70 people, including world leaders and major figures in global conflicts. In addition to Netanyahu, it has sought the arrest of Hamas figures. Others who were the subject of arrest warrants include Russian President Vladimir Putin, former Sudan President Omar al-Bashir and former Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi. Charges against Kenyan President William Ruto and former Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta were withdrawn. NOBEL COMMITTEE CITES POLITICAL ATTACKS IN AWARDING PRIZE Despite [USN:L6N45G1AB TEXT:"US calls for countries to quit the court"], it has received strong backing from most member states, which include all EU countries and all members of the NATO alliance apart from the United States and Turkey. It is based in the Netherlands, an EU and NATO member. The Nobel Prize awarded hours earlier to South African jurist Navi Pillay, who sat on the ICC's Appeals Chamber from 2003-2008, was explicitly described by the prize committee as a gesture of support for such tribunals at a time when "judges and institutions of international law are under political attack". "An international legal system in which war criminals are held to account and the victims of abuse see justice served is a precondition for a peaceful world," the prize committee said. US sanctions typically bar all US-based companies from any work with a sanctioned organization, forcing banks to shut accounts, insurers to end coverage and software companies to halt cooperation. The Trump administration previously imposed targeted sanctions on court officials during his first term, which were rescinded under President Joe Biden. Washington announced new sanctions just days after Trump returned to office in January 2025. Court officials have been preparing for months for the prospect of [USN:L6N45D0HW TEXT:"sanctions on the court"] itself, shifting office computers from Microsoft software to open-source equivalents and making new arrangements for banking and health insurance.

item.title: Merz 'outraged' that German former Chancellor Schroeder attended Putin's birthday
item.description: Gerhard Schroeder has faced criticism over his links to Russian businesses and Putin.
item.dc:creator: Emanuele Berro, Friederike Heine
item.content:encoded: Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz is "deeply outraged" by former Chancellor Gerhard Schroeder's [USN:L8N45U2DQ TEXT:"visit"] to Vladimir Putin's home to celebrate the Russian president's birthday this week, a German government spokesperson said on Friday. Schroeder, who served as chancellor from 1998 to 2005, has faced criticism in Germany and abroad over his links to Russian business and Putin, ties that have persisted despite Moscow's 2022 invasion of Ukraine and subsequent waves of Western sanctions. "Putin alone is responsible for the war in Ukraine. His orders are the cause of immeasurable suffering, civilian casualties, families being torn apart, dead and wounded," the spokesperson said. "The chancellor sees ... it as downright immoral for Mr. Schroeder to attend such a celebration." Putin turned 74 on Thursday. Schroeder, 82, and his wife, So-Yeon Schroeder-Kim, who sometimes handles his communications, did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment. The visit also drew criticism from within Schroeder's own Social Democratic Party (SPD). The party's co-leader Lars Klingbeil, who is also Germany's finance minister in Merz's conservative-led coalition, called it "completely unacceptable" in view of the suffering caused to Ukraine's people, according to the Sueddeutsche Zeitung daily. Schroeder has been appointed to several high-ranking positions in Russian companies in the last 20 years. Shortly after stepping down, he became chairman of the shareholders' committee of Nord Stream, the Gazprom-led Baltic Sea pipeline project he had championed while in office, and later held senior positions at Russian oil producer Rosneft. Earlier this year, Putin said Schroeder would be his preferred interlocutor for talks on new security arrangements for Europe, an idea immediately rejected by the European Union and Merz's government. Last week, Schroeder joined the supervisory board of Russian retailer Hyperglobus, a spin-off of Germany's Globus Holding which operates more than 20 supermarkets in Russia.

item.title: Paris jitters, oil battles and a Bolsonaro-fuelled Brazil rally: The financial week in five charts
item.description: Every Friday, Reuters Open Interest distills the financial week into five key charts, spotlighting the major trends, surprises and overlooked moves that defined the past five days.
item.dc:creator: Anna Szymanski
item.content:encoded: Every Friday, Reuters Open Interest (ROI) distills the financial week into five key charts, spotlighting the major trends, surprises and overlooked moves that defined the past five days. 1. FRENCH FRACTURE MIKE DOLAN, ROI Finance & Markets Columnist: A surge of market anxiety over France's budget deficits and upcoming elections has seen French government borrowing rates and risk premia versus Germany rise to levels not seen since the heat of the euro crisis in 2011. This has weighed on other euro sovereign spreads and banking stocks while also sending the euro to an [USN:L4N45T025 TEXT:"18-month low"] against the dollar. A euro crisis redux with France at its centre would be expected to elicit a major European Central Bank response to contain spillovers and insulate the single currency. But a looming leadership change at the top of the central bank could [USN:L6N45R0YE TEXT:"complicate that process"] and potentially raise the bar for action. 2. INFLECTION POINT? JAMIE MCGEEVER, ROI Markets Columnist: The big question in markets right now is whether we may be [USN:L6N45U02K TEXT:"at, or near, an inflection point"]. The spiking "term premium" is one example, as it threatens to slam both stocks and bonds. The term premium is the estimated level of extra compensation investors demand in return for buying long-dated Treasuries over short-term debt. What's pushing it higher remains an open question: growing doubts about Federal Reserve credibility, fears of US debt debasement, or something else entirely. But whatever the cause, the central concern is whether it keeps rising. If it does, that may signal some serious economic and market problems ahead. 3. LET THE BATTLE COMMENCE RON BOUSSO, ROI Energy Columnist: Middle East oil producers have launched a battle to [USN:L6N45T150 TEXT:"recapture market share"] lost during the Iran war. The scramble to recover lost customers is becoming a defining feature of the post-blockade market. Gulf producers, eager to replenish state coffers after more than seven months of disruption, are increasing exports while some producers, including Iraq and [USN:S8N45108K TEXT:"Saudi Arabia"], have [USN:L1N45N03W TEXT:"offered deep discounts"] to buyers willing to load cargoes inside the Gulf. But will this tussle for market share result in dramatically lower prices at the pump? Probably not as long as getting oil through Hormuz remains [USN:L6N45Q087 TEXT:"risky, unpredictable and expensive"]. 4. BOLSONARO BOOST JAMIE MCGEEVER, ROI Markets Columnist: That rumbling beneath emerging market investors' feet may be the first tremors of what could be a political earthquake in Brazil. Right-wing candidate Flavio Bolsonaro — son of former President [USN:S0N42U07U TEXT:"Jair Bolsonaro"], who in 2025 was convicted of plotting a coup to remain in power after losing the 2022 election — did much better than expected in the first round of voting in Sunday's presidential election. From a financial markets viewpoint, at least, the [USN:L1N45R09E TEXT:"verdict"] is clear: investors seem pleased with the potential turn to the right. The sizzling rally in Brazilian assets (.BVSP) and the real on Monday says it all. 5. SERIOUSNESS DEFICIT? ANNA SZYMANSKI, ROI Editor-in-Charge: Most US voters believe the Trump administration, Congress and AI companies are not taking AI risks seriously enough, [USN:L6N45S14D TEXT:"according to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll"]. AI risks have become a hot-button US political issue amid workers' fears about job security, local opposition to data centers and even warnings from AI labs that the technology could pose an existential threat to humanity. President Donald Trump has continued to double down on support for what he calls "Super Intelligence" and the data-center infrastructure it requires, arguing that the US cannot afford to fall behind China in this tech race. With the midterm elections approaching, that support could become a liability for Republican candidates in tight races. Opinions expressed are those of the authors. item.title: Hurricane Simon strengthens off Mexico's Pacific coast, threatens tourist region
item.description: The storm is churning toward a coastline dotted with beach resorts and fishing towns.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Becerril
item.content:encoded: Hurricane Simon is rapidly intensifying off Mexico's Pacific coast, packing sustained winds of 110 mph (177 kph) as it churns toward a stretch of coastline dotted with beach resorts and fishing towns, the US National Hurricane Center said on Friday. Simon, nearing Category 3 strength, is forecast to become a dangerous Category 4 by Saturday as it approaches Mexico's southwestern and west-central Pacific coast, one of the country's most popular tourist regions, the NHC said. "Simon could deliver the most significant hurricane impact to this stretch of the Mexican Pacific coast since Lidia in 2023, which damaged thousands of homes and devastated crops along the Jalisco coast," said Tyler Roys, a senior meteorologist at AccuWeather. Simon is expected to make landfall on Sunday between Manzanillo — Mexico’s largest port and the main gateway for trade with Asia — and Puerto Vallarta, a popular beach destination and home to nearly 300,000 residents. In Manzanillo, fishermen were hauling their boats off the beach and authorities were putting up black flags along the coast to signal the beach was closed. The Mexican Navy activated emergency response personnel in Colima and restricted maritime traffic along parts of the Pacific coast, closing ports to smaller vessels and barring larger vessels from operating in Michoacan. Simon was about 195 miles (315 km) south of Manzanillo in the afternoon and crawling northwest, according to the NHC. Forecasters warned that Simon could bring life-threatening flooding and mudslides, with isolated rainfall totals reaching 30 inches (762 mm) in parts of Michoacan, Colima, Jalisco and Nayarit. Mexican authorities warned that heavy rainfall was expected in the states of Guerrero, Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco. [USN:L8N45L0P6 TEXT:"Last week"], Hurricane Polo made landfall on the Baja California Peninsula as a Category 2 storm, toppling trees and utility poles, flooding streets and causing other property damage.

item.title: Ukraine hits second major tech site, expanding range of targets inside Russia
item.description: Ukraine is widening the scope of its attacks inside Russia.
item.dc:creator: Mark Trevelyan, Gleb Stolyarov
item.content:encoded: Ukraine struck and partly disabled a major data centre operated by Russian technology company Yandex on Friday in the second such action in successive days, widening the scope of its attacks inside Russia after Moscow hit data hubs in Ukraine . Yandex, which is heavily involved in Russia's AI development and is sometimes called Russia's Google, said its data centre in the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow had been struck by Ukrainian drones and partly put out of action. Ukrainian arms maker Firepoint said Kyiv had used its FP-1 one-way attack drones to mount the strike against what it called Yandex's biggest data centre and said that several of its modules had been completely knocked out of action. A day earlier, a Ukrainian attack [USN:L8N45U1P7 TEXT:"shut down Yandex's data hub in Sasovo"], southeast of Moscow, where two of the three supercomputers used to develop the company's AI model are housed. Yandex said it was facing a difficult challenge to maintain its services, used by millions of Russians daily for navigation, music, movies, food orders and other tasks. It also provides cloud computing services on which many businesses depend. YANDEX SHARES FALL ON RUSSIAN EXCHANGE Alexander Savitsky, who runs a start-up dating app called Pulse with 8,000 users, told Reuters that none of them had been able to access it since Thursday. He said the company was unable to reach its backup database in Yandex Cloud and was getting an "internal error" message when trying to restore it elsewhere. "We have no confirmation of actual data loss, but the situation is serious: the project represents three years of work," Savitsky said. "The main risk is losing users and their trust: people can't use the app, and there's no telling how many will return once service is restored." Yandex said it had struck a deal with other cloud providers to enable clients to swiftly move their data and services. Its shares fell by more than 4% on the Moscow exchange. "The risks involve not only the potential temporary unavailability of Yandex services and lost revenue in specific segments but also the company's extensive base of B2B clients," said Maryana Lazaricheva, head of equity research at T-Investments. She said the company could redistribute some of the load to its other data centres. "However, if the chain of attacks continues, this possibility vanishes, which could lead to even more severe consequences." BOTH SIDES EXPAND RANGE OF ECONOMIC TARGETS Locked in a deadly [USN:L1N45U0VZ TEXT:"war of attrition"] after more than four years of fighting, both Russia and Ukraine have expanded drone attacks this year on infrastructure targets, from energy facilities and refineries to ports and vessels carrying oil and grain, [USN:L1N44L05J TEXT:"e-commerce warehouses"] and, most recently, data centres. The full scale of the disruption caused by the attacks was not immediately clear, although messages appeared on at least one Yandex app warning of potential problems in its operation. Yandex said it was working around the clock to try to restore services which had been disrupted. "Right now this is our most important task, but unfortunately it is not an easy one," it said. Russia has struck Ukrainian data centres and telecommunications infrastructure over the past month, including targets in central Kyiv. "We always respond in mirror-like fashion," Ukrainian President [USN:L1N45U08A TEXT:"Volodymyr Zelenskiy"] said on Thursday. He confirmed on Friday that his drones had struck the Kaluga data centre in what he called "our tit-for-tat response". The regional governor said nine people had been injured in Ukraine's attacks, five of whom were being treated in hospital. SPARTAK MOSCOW AMONG WEBSITES CITING DIFFICULTIES Ukraine has previously targeted the warehouses of specific companies it deems central to Russia's economy, including dozens of sites operated by e-commerce giants Wildberries and Ozon. Russia responded by striking their Ukrainian equivalents. Yandex operates five data centres, two of which have already been hit. It said in 2021 that the Sasovo data hub, which was struck on Thursday, hosted two of its three supercomputers built around Nvidia A100 chips, which it uses to train its YandexGPT large AI model. Yandex has declined to say whether the supercomputers were affected by the attack. Multiple online services in Russia reported technical issues on Thursday, including real estate aggregator Cian, a book portal called Litmarket, and the websites of Russian Railways and professional football club Spartak Moscow. Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centres have forced some of them to suspend operations, while 100,000 households suffered temporary internet outages after one attack. Ukraine's digital minister told Reuters last month that the country was responding by moving digital infrastructure underground.

item.title: Central banks face test. Will they be good cops or bond villains?
item.description: A standoff between the banks and their governments may come as a bond-market crunch reopens questions about the political independence of the banks.
item.dc:creator: Mike Dolan
item.content:encoded: A standoff between central banks and their cash-strapped governments may well be looming as an intensifying [USN:L6N45U0LN TEXT:"bond market crunch"] reopens questions about the political independence of the banks well beyond their interest-rate policy. Central banks currently appear reluctant to rebuild holdings of sovereign debt, yet those holdings played a significant role in the swelling public borrowing over the past decade. Moving forward, that means either an improbable fiscal tightening will need to emerge or political knives will be sharpened. Numerous elections in the US, France, Italy and Spain over the coming year mean significant spending cuts are unlikely to be on the agenda. If bond markets continue to tighten — as we've seen in recent weeks — political pressure on central banks to steady the ship will rise even further. Seeing the problem coming like a slow-motion car crash, central banks are trying to nuance their position. On one hand, a post-pandemic consensus has built around further "normalization" of their bond-packed balance sheets. This includes a retrospective disdain for using bond accumulation as a monetary policy tool. On the other hand, policymakers want to keep all options open for temporary fixes in the event of market malfunctioning or another left-field shock. Bank for International Settlements (BIS) boss Pablo Hernandez de Cos this week laid out some principles for using emergency tools if conditions get rough, using the example of the Bank of England's (BoE) limited and brief support for stressed British gilts during the budget blow-up in 2022. "A key challenge is to bolster market confidence without overstimulating the economy in the longer term," he said of such emergency tools. "Central banks should try to better distinguish programmes for market functioning from those for monetary stimulus." But the problem with a middle-ground, [USN:L6N45T16X TEXT:"only-in-emergencies"] approach is that sometimes debt markets can get squeezed even when there isn't an acute crisis. Just look at the current global bond selloff. Markets are not necessarily malfunctioning, and despite the clear energy hit from the Iran war , there's no global shock on the scale of COVID-19 or the 2008 banking crash to justify a red alert. Yet markets continue to inflict maximum pain on government debt-service bills. Should this continue, alongside a relatively hot AI-infused economy and above-target inflation rates, monetary policymakers could find themselves in a very tough spot. If central banks do step in, the lines between "backstops," monetary policy and direct government support could become blurred, and central bankers could once again find themselves criticised for enabling rising government debt loads. Yet governments across the developed world may expect them to do just that if sovereign bond yields keep increasing. Rising debt-service bills are coming at a time when ageing demographics in most Group of Seven (G7) economies have already been heaping pressure on pension and healthcare systems, while defence spending is set to spiral higher amid increasingly fraught geopolitics. Pointing to forecasts that global government debt will exceed annual global GDP by 2030, [USN:L1N45S0Z3 TEXT:"International Monetary Fund head Kristalina Georgieva"] this week warned rich governments to deliver credible fiscal-consolidation plans urgently and not fall back on central banks to bail them out. "I would call this 'monetary cowboys', running to the rescue of the fiscal agents, and my message is: please don't." HOW DID WE GET HERE? For context, we need to rewind a bit. Of the multiple reasons cited for the intense government bond market selloff in recent months, a big question revolves around the gaping hole left in debt markets by the gradual withdrawal of G7 central banks from the swelling debt piles they facilitated following 2008. The selloff has pushed long-term US sovereign borrowing costs to their highest in almost a quarter of a century. Perhaps the best way to understand how artificially cheap borrowing distorted the picture is to examine how quickly governments accumulated debt when their central banks were buying bonds and effectively underwriting large chunks of it. The Washington-based Institute of International Finance recently estimated that even though average government borrowing costs across the G7 are back at mid-2008 levels, annual interest expenses are 85% higher because G7 government debts have almost trebled to more than $60 trillion in the interim. Advanced economies collectively are now paying over $3.3 trillion to service bonds alone, it said, which is more than their estimated spending on either AI, defence or clean energy. But coinciding with, and aggravating, the recent surge in government debt costs has been the steady pruning of central bank balance sheets over the past four years. The aggregate G7 central bank balance sheet peaked at over $30 trillion of bonds in early 2022 and has been cut by about a third since then.Along with the sharp rise in central bank policy rates to choke off inflation, that one-third reduction has coincided with a 40% drop in long-term G7 government bond indexes and a four-percentage-point spike in their implied borrowing rate. Have central banks exited too much or too quickly, and should they pause that withdrawal until they rethink it? BALANCE SHEET PHILOSOPHY Opinion on the wisdom of so-called quantitative easing (QE) — massive central-bank bond-buying programs — has done an almost 180-degree turn since the inflation spikes and debt explosions of the pandemic and its aftermath. For many, the banking crash of 2008 and 2020's COVID-19 lockdowns justified extraordinary one-off balance sheet reactions from the Federal Reserve and others. But many also now criticize the continuous use of bond buying as an ongoing monetary tool, arguing that it underwrote the massive expansion of government debt over the past 20 years. Much of the central bank world now feels the experiment may have been misguided at best, both because it tiptoed into quasi-fiscal territory and because of a variety of market distortions and inequality questions that arose from what was essentially direct support for wealthier asset owners. New Fed Chair and long-time balance-sheet-expansion sceptic [USN:S8N40E0AX TEXT:"Kevin Warsh "]claims the whole 18-year QE episode "borders on fiscal policy." He has already set up one of his Fed reform task forces to look at ways to reduce the balance sheet holdings further. On the other side of the pond, the [USN:L8N4590WV TEXT:"BoE"] is still actively selling gilts, albeit with recent plans to concentrate sales in short-dated paper. And the European Central Bank is still actively running down its balance sheet, which amounts to more than 40% of euro zone GDP, even as the region faces echoes of the 2011-12 euro debt crisis in French bond markets. A change of [USN:L6N45R0YE TEXT:"ECB leadership"] is also on the horizon, and the leading candidates don't appear to have an appetite for a return to the 2010s and the firefighting activism of former chief Mario Draghi. TWITCHIER TREASURIES There is also the question of who is holding government debt. The reduction of G7 central bank bond holdings has coincided with reduced pension-fund demand for long-dated government debt as defined-benefit schemes dwindle and pension savers retire. Those gaps left by long-term investors keen on safety and steady coupons have increasingly been filled by more speculative, short-term players such as hedge funds, who are much more sensitive to big price shifts, vulnerable to short-term interest rate changes and prone to herding in volatile conditions. Hedge fund activity in sovereign bond markets has been the focus of regulators for years. While everyone welcomes the demand and liquidity they provide, there is now growing concern about the flipside of that if this "fast money" base gets twitchy. Some efforts have been made to reduce [USN:L6N45R0WM TEXT:"excessive leverage"] in government bond markets, but no matter how that pans out, the scale of [USN:L6N44U0ZU TEXT:"hedge fund activity"] in these markets, and by extension the exposure of the banks and trading houses that provide them with leverage, makes for a more skittish environment. "These buyers are more inclined to sell bonds in response to higher short-term interest rates — funding leg sensitivity — and charge a higher price for the risk of further upward moves," wrote Carlyle strategist Jason Thomas. "When coupled with the growth in the outstanding volume of debt, this new class of investors has left bond markets more fragile and sensitized to front-end repricing." This sensitivity helps to explain the recent disturbance in Treasury markets, which seems to have been driven largely by the Fed changing course on short-term rates. SMBC Nikko's rates strategist Joseph Abate cites Fed studies trying to quantify that sensitivity. Fed economist Phillip Monin estimates that hedge fund demand for [USN:L1N45E0NO TEXT:"cash-futures arbitrage plays "]has increased fourfold since 2020 and is now 3.5% of outstanding Treasury supply. Another Fed study last month by Daniel Beltran and Canlin Li found that the market's sensitivity to new supply had doubled over the past decade, with every 1% increase in new debt, some $300 billion or more, increasing 5-year yields by 8 basis points. Regulators, governments and central banks are watching this closely. But any planned tightening of rules could well have adverse effects at a politically risky moment. While the answer, in theory, may be reducing the supply of government debt, in practice, that is very unlikely to occur. The alternative solution lands back in the lap of now more hesitant central banks — kicking and screaming perhaps. (The opinions expressed here are those of Mike Dolan , a columnist for Reuters.) item.title: Mali troops re-enter strategic northern town after separatists withdraw
item.description: It is a symbolic boost to Mali's army and its Russian backers.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: A separatist movement in northern Mali announced on Tuesday it was carrying out "a controlled withdrawal" from a strategic town in the north, a symbolic boost to Mali's army and its Russian backers in their years-long fight against insurgents including al Qaeda-linked jihadists. Malian troops were "reinforcing their presence" in the town by Tuesday night, a government statement said, adding that this would allow for "the gradual return of public administration and basic social services". The Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) took control of Kidal town six months ago in [USN:L6N41903L TEXT:"nationwide attacks"] that also killed Mali's defence minister. It had joined forces in those attacks with the regional al Qaeda affiliate, Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin, known as JNIM, posing the biggest test yet to Mali's military leaders who seized power in coups in 2020 and 2021. The FLA's decision to leave Kidal came in response to airstrikes by Mali's military backed by Russian fighters, the FLA said in a statement. "The FLA specifies that this is a temporary operational measure, also intended to preserve its human and logistical capabilities intact. This methodical withdrawal from the area took place without any direct combat having yet pitted its forces against the enemy," the statement said. Mali has leaned on Russian security support for years, first from the Wagner mercenary group and then from the paramilitary group Africa Corps, which is made up of many former Wagner fighters. 'SYMBOLIC' BUT NOT DECISIVE VICTORY, ANALYST SAYS Earlier on Tuesday, Mali's military said it had launched large-scale air and ground operations in the region of Kidal. The goals of the operations included tracking down and neutralizing armed groups operating in the area, destroying their supply networks and restoring "lasting security" and free movement for people and goods, a Malian military statement said. Pro-government fighters, including Russian fighters, re-entered Kidal on Tuesday afternoon, a security source said. Malian forces and Wagner fighters retook Kidal from insurgents in November 2023, the most concrete gain from their partnership — only to lose it during the attacks in April. "A successful recapture... affirms the military-led government's authority and boosts the army's morale, particularly after several high-profile setbacks both in the north and the central regions in recent weeks," said Beverly Ochieng, associate director of Control Risks. "This is also an opportunity for Africa Corps to reprise its role as the Malian government's security guarantor after appearing to lose significant ground, including in Kidal, since April." But the change of control in Kidal is still largely "symbolic" and not "decisive" in Mali's campaign against insurgent groups, Ochieng added. A source close to the FLA leadership told Reuters that the aerial operations by Malian and Russian forces began three days ago. The source played down the significance of the FLA's withdrawal, saying it was a measure to protect lives and equipment. "For us, war is not a race against the clock," the source said.
